units.label: Atoms, Bonding, and the Structure of Matter

lessons.label: The Atom: Structure, Isotopes, and the Nucleus

sections.heading: Protons, Neutrons, Electrons, and the Nuclear Model
sections.body: Every atom is built from three subatomic particles: protons (charge +1, mass ~1 amu) and neutrons (charge 0, mass ~1 amu) packed into a tiny central nucleus, and electrons (charge -1, mass ~1/1836 amu) occupying the much larger volume around it. Ernest Rutherford's 1909 gold foil experiment, run by his students Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, overturned J.J. Thomson's diffuse "plum pudding" model. Alpha particles fired at gold foil only 0.00004 cm thick mostly passed straight through, but a small fraction -- roughly 1 in 8,000 for thick metal foils, though the ratio is foil-dependent and Rutherford's own 1911 analysis for gold put it closer to 1 in 20,000 -- bounced back at angles greater than 90 degrees. Rutherford called this "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you," concluding that positive charge and nearly all the mass must be concentrated in a nucleus roughly 100,000 times smaller than the atom itself.

sections.heading: Atomic Number, Mass Number, and Isotopes
sections.body: The atomic number (Z) equals the number of protons and defines the element; carbon is carbon because Z = 6, no matter how many neutrons it has. The mass number (A) is the sum of protons plus neutrons in a specific atom, written as a superscript (carbon-12, or 12C). Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different neutron counts and therefore different mass numbers. Carbon has three natural isotopes: carbon-12 (98.9% abundance, 6 neutrons), carbon-13 (1.1%, 7 neutrons), and radioactive carbon-14 (trace, 8 neutrons, half-life 5,730 years, the basis of radiocarbon dating). The average atomic mass on the periodic table, 12.011 for carbon, is a weighted average over natural abundances, not the mass of any single real atom.

sections.heading: Ions and Charge Imbalance
sections.body: An atom is electrically neutral only when protons equal electrons. Ions form when an atom gains or loses electrons (the proton count, and therefore identity, never changes in ordinary chemical reactions). Losing electrons gives a cation with a net positive charge, e.g., Na loses one electron to form Na+, matching the stable electron configuration of neon. Gaining electrons gives an anion with a net negative charge, e.g., Cl gains one electron to form Cl-, matching argon's configuration. The number of protons stays fixed at 11 for sodium and 17 for chlorine throughout; only the electron count changes, which is why ionization is chemical, not nuclear.

lessons.workedExample: A sample of naturally occurring chlorine is 75.77% chlorine-35 (mass 34.969 amu) and 24.23% chlorine-37 (mass 36.966 amu). The average atomic mass is (0.7577 x 34.969) + (0.2423 x 36.966) = 26.496 + 8.957 = 35.453 amu, matching the periodic table value of 35.45. Now consider the chloride ion Cl-: it still has 17 protons (Z = 17, so it is still chlorine) but 18 electrons, giving it a net charge of -1 and the same electron configuration as argon (18 electrons), even though its nucleus differs from argon's by one proton.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student can cleanly separate three different quantities that students often blur together: atomic number (identity), mass number (a specific atom's nucleon count), and average atomic mass (a weighted statistic over isotopes). A strong answer explains why isotopes of the same element behave almost identically chemically (same electron count and configuration) while differing in mass and nuclear stability, and correctly states that forming an ion changes electron count, never proton count. A weak answer conflates mass number with average atomic mass, or claims ionization changes what element an atom is.

questions.prompt: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons, and 18 electrons. What is true of this atom?

options.text: It is a neutral atom of chlorine-35
It is a chloride ion, Cl-, with mass number 35
It is a neutral atom of argon-35
It is a chloride ion, Cl-, with mass number 36

explanations.a: 17 protons but 18 electrons means the charges do not balance, so this cannot be a neutral atom; it is an ion.
explanations.b: Correct: Z = 17 identifies chlorine; protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35 gives mass number 35; 18 electrons versus 17 protons gives a net charge of -1, i.e., Cl-.
explanations.c: Argon has 18 protons (Z = 18), not 17, so this element is chlorine, not argon.
explanations.d: The mass number is protons + neutrons = 17 + 18 = 35, not 36; the electron count does not add to the mass number.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the historical development of the nuclear atomic model, earliest first.

items.text: Thomson proposes the plum pudding model with electrons embedded in diffuse positive charge
Rutherford, Geiger, and Marsden fire alpha particles at gold foil and observe some scatter backward
Rutherford proposes a small, dense, positively charged nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance

questions.explanation: Thomson's model came first (1904); the gold foil scattering experiment (1909, analyzed 1911) produced the anomalous backscattering data; Rutherford's nuclear model was the explanation he proposed to account for that data.

questions.prompt: Match each particle to its approximate relative mass and charge.

right.text: ~1 amu, charge +1
~1 amu, charge 0
~1/1836 amu, charge -1

questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons each have a mass of roughly 1 amu, but protons carry +1 charge and neutrons are neutral; electrons are about 1836 times lighter than a proton and carry -1 charge.

lessons.label: Electron Configuration and Quantum Numbers

sections.heading: Orbitals and the Shapes That Hold Electrons
sections.body: Electrons do not orbit the nucleus like planets; quantum mechanics describes them with orbitals, three-dimensional regions where an electron is likely to be found, derived from solutions to the Schrodinger equation published in 1926. Each orbital is labeled by a subshell type: s orbitals are spherical and hold up to 2 electrons; p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped and come in sets of three (holding up to 6 electrons); d orbitals come in sets of five (up to 10 electrons); f orbitals come in sets of seven (up to 14 electrons). The principal quantum number n (1, 2, 3...) sets the energy level and rough size of the orbital, while the subshell letter sets its shape and orientation options.

sections.heading: Three Rules for Filling Orbitals
sections.body: The Aufbau principle states electrons fill lowest-energy orbitals first, following the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and so on -- notably 4s fills before 3d despite the smaller principal quantum number, because 4s is lower in energy for neutral atoms in the ground state. The Pauli exclusion principle, proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, states no two electrons in the same atom can share all four quantum numbers; practically, this means each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, and they must have opposite spins. Hund's rule states that when filling a set of degenerate orbitals (like the three 2p orbitals), electrons occupy separate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing occurs -- this minimizes electron-electron repulsion and is why nitrogen's three 2p electrons sit one each in 2px, 2py, 2pz rather than pairing up.

sections.heading: Valence Electrons and the Periodic Table's Block Shape
sections.body: Valence electrons -- those in the outermost occupied shell (highest n) plus any partially filled d or f subshells contributing to bonding -- determine an element's chemical behavior, which is why elements in the same group share similar reactivity. The periodic table's very shape encodes the orbital-filling order: the two leftmost columns (groups 1-2) are the s-block, where the outermost s orbital fills; the six rightmost columns (groups 13-18) are the p-block; the ten-column middle section (transition metals) is the d-block, filling n-1 d orbitals; and the two 14-column rows pulled below the main table are the f-block (lanthanides and actinides), filling n-2 f orbitals. Oxygen (1s2 2s2 2p4) has 6 valence electrons, all in n=2, giving it the same reactive pattern as sulfur and selenium below it in group 16.

lessons.workedExample: Write the ground-state electron configuration for iron (Z = 26). Following Aufbau order: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 4s2 3d6, which totals 2+2+6+2+6+2+6 = 26 electrons. Note 4s fills before 3d, but once both are occupied, 4s electrons are actually higher in energy and are the ones removed first when iron ionizes -- so Fe2+ has configuration [Ar] 3d6, not [Ar] 4s2 3d4. The five 3d orbitals (in [Ar]3d6, one orbital holds a pair and four hold single electrons) fill according to Hund's rule: each of the five 3d orbitals gets one electron before any doubles up, except the sixth electron must pair since all five orbitals already hold one each.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student actually understands why the filling order and the periodic table's shape are the same fact seen two ways, not memorized separately. A strong answer can derive a given element's configuration from its position on the table (block and period) and correctly apply Hund's rule to predict how many unpaired electrons a partially filled subshell has, and knows that 4s electrons ionize before 3d despite filling first. A weak answer recites configurations by rote without being able to explain the aufbau exception, or misapplies Hund's rule by pairing electrons before every degenerate orbital has one.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes Hund's rule as applied to filling the three 2p orbitals with electrons?

options.text: Electrons pair up in one 2p orbital before any other 2p orbital is used
Electrons occupy each of the three 2p orbitals singly, with parallel spin, before any pairing occurs
Electrons fill 2p orbitals in a random, unpredictable order
Electrons must fill 2s completely before any 2p orbital can be used, which is a separate rule from Hund's rule

explanations.a: This is the opposite of Hund's rule; pairing before singly occupying every degenerate orbital raises electron-electron repulsion and is energetically unfavorable.
explanations.b: Correct: Hund's rule minimizes repulsion by spreading electrons across degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing begins.
explanations.c: Orbital filling is governed by well-defined rules (Aufbau, Pauli, Hund), not randomness.
explanations.d: Filling 2s before 2p is the Aufbau principle (lower energy first), a distinct rule from Hund's, which concerns degenerate orbitals of the same subshell.

questions.prompt: Order these subshells by the sequence in which they fill according to the Aufbau principle.

items.text: 3p
4s
3d
4p

questions.explanation: The Aufbau filling order proceeds 3p, then 4s (lower energy than 3d for neutral ground-state atoms), then 3d, then 4p.

questions.prompt: Match each orbital type to the maximum number of electrons its full set can hold.

right.text: 2 electrons
6 electrons
10 electrons
14 electrons

questions.explanation: Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons (Pauli exclusion), and a subshell's orbital count sets its total capacity: 1x2=2 for s, 3x2=6 for p, 5x2=10 for d, 7x2=14 for f.

lessons.label: Periodic Trends

sections.heading: Effective Nuclear Charge and Shielding: The Engine Behind Every Trend
sections.body: Nearly all periodic trends trace back to two competing effects. Effective nuclear charge (Zeff), approximated by Slater's rules as Zeff = Z - S, is the net positive pull an outer electron actually feels after inner electrons partially cancel (shield) the full nuclear charge. Moving left to right across a period, protons are added to the nucleus while electrons are added to the same outer shell, which shields poorly against each other -- so Zeff rises steadily (for period 2, Zeff felt by valence electrons rises from about 1.3 for lithium to about 5.85 for neon). Moving down a group, each new period adds a full inner shell of shielding electrons, so Zeff on the valence shell stays roughly constant even as the actual nuclear charge Z grows, but the valence electrons sit in a higher, larger shell farther from the nucleus.

sections.heading: Atomic Radius and Ionization Energy
sections.body: Atomic radius shrinks left to right across a period, because rising Zeff pulls the same-shell electrons in tighter (Li, 152 pm, down to a much smaller Ne), and it grows down a group as each period adds an entire new shell (Li 152 pm to Cs 265 pm). Ionization energy -- the energy to remove the outermost electron -- runs opposite to radius: it rises left to right (Li 520 kJ/mol to Ne 2081 kJ/mol) because higher Zeff and a smaller radius both make the electron harder to remove, and it falls down a group (Li 520 kJ/mol to Cs 376 kJ/mol) because the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded. Nitrogen is a notable exception to the smooth rise: its half-filled 2p3 configuration (one electron in each of the three 2p orbitals) is extra stable, so nitrogen's ionization energy (1402 kJ/mol) is slightly higher than oxygen's (1314 kJ/mol), reversing the expected order.

sections.heading: Electron Affinity and Electronegativity
sections.body: Electron affinity, the energy change when an atom gains an electron, generally becomes more negative (more energy released, stronger pull) left to right across a period as Zeff rises, and less negative down a group. Halogens have the most negative electron affinities (chlorine, -349 kJ/mol) because adding one electron completes a stable octet. Electronegativity, Linus Pauling's 1932 scale of an atom's pull on shared bonding electrons, combines both radius and Zeff effects and follows the same overall pattern: it rises left to right and falls down a group. Fluorine is the most electronegative element at 3.98 on the Pauling scale, and electronegativity is the single most useful number for predicting bond type, since the difference between two atoms' electronegativities predicts whether a bond will be nonpolar covalent, polar covalent, or ionic.

lessons.workedExample: Compare sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), and chlorine (Cl), all period 3. Across the period, Zeff rises (Na ~2.2, Cl ~6.1 by Slater estimates), so atomic radius shrinks (Na 186 pm, Mg 160 pm, Cl 99 pm) and ionization energy rises (Na 496 kJ/mol, Mg 738 kJ/mol, Cl 1251 kJ/mol). Electronegativity also rises left to right (Na 0.93, Mg 1.31, Cl 3.16 on the Pauling scale). This is why NaCl forms an ionic bond (electronegativity difference 3.16 - 0.93 = 2.23, a large gap favoring electron transfer) while a Mg-Cl bond, though still fairly ionic, has a smaller gap (3.16 - 1.31 = 1.85) than Na-Cl.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student can explain WHY a trend exists (Zeff and shielding), not just recite that it exists. A strong answer connects radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, and electronegativity back to the same two underlying causes and can flag exceptions like nitrogen's anomalously high ionization energy from its half-filled 2p3 stability. A weak answer states the trend directions correctly but cannot explain the mechanism, or cannot predict bond character from an electronegativity difference.

questions.prompt: Why does atomic radius decrease moving left to right across a period, despite protons and electrons both increasing?

options.text: Electrons added within the same shell shield each other poorly, so effective nuclear charge rises and pulls the shell in tighter
A new electron shell is added at each step, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus
Electron-electron repulsion increases so much that electrons are pushed away from the nucleus, shrinking the atom
The number of neutrons decreases across a period, reducing the nuclear pull

explanations.a: Correct: same-shell electrons shield each other weakly, so rising nuclear charge is not fully offset, effective nuclear charge increases, and the valence shell is pulled in tighter.
explanations.b: No new shell is added across a period; that only happens moving down a group to a new principal quantum number.
explanations.c: Repulsion among same-shell electrons is real but is outweighed by the rising nuclear pull; the net effect is a smaller radius, not a larger one.
explanations.d: Neutron count does not follow a simple pattern across a period and neutrons do not significantly affect electron shielding, which is an electron-electron effect.

questions.prompt: Order these elements from smallest to largest first ionization energy: Cs, Cl, Na, F.

items.text: Cs
Na
Cl
F

questions.explanation: Cs (376 kJ/mol) is a large, heavily shielded alkali metal at the bottom of group 1, lowest ionization energy; Na (496 kJ/mol) is a smaller alkali metal one period up; Cl (1251 kJ/mol) is a period-3 halogen with high Zeff; F (1681 kJ/mol) is a period-2 halogen, smaller and less shielded than Cl, giving it the highest ionization energy of the four.

questions.prompt: Match each periodic trend to its direction moving left to right across a period.

right.text: Decreases
Increases
Increases

questions.explanation: Rising effective nuclear charge across a period pulls electrons in tighter (radius decreases) and makes them harder to remove (ionization energy increases) and more strongly attracted in a shared bond (electronegativity increases).

lessons.label: Chemical Bonding: Ionic, Covalent, and Metallic

sections.heading: Why Bonds Form: Electronegativity Difference as the Deciding Factor
sections.body: Atoms bond because sharing or transferring electrons lowers the total energy of the system relative to separate atoms, generally moving each atom toward a filled valence shell. Which type of bond forms is predicted mainly by the electronegativity difference between the two atoms involved, using rough Pauling-scale cutoffs: a difference greater than about 1.7-2.0 typically means ionic bonding (electrons are transferred essentially completely, as in NaCl, difference 2.23); a difference between about 0.4 and 1.7 means polar covalent bonding (electrons are shared unequally, as in H-Cl, difference 0.96); and a difference below about 0.4 means nonpolar covalent bonding (electrons are shared roughly equally, as in C-H, difference 0.35, or Cl-Cl, difference 0). These cutoffs are guidelines, not hard boundaries -- bonding character is a continuous spectrum, not three discrete boxes.

sections.heading: Ionic Bonding and Lattice Energy
sections.body: Ionic bonds form between a metal (low ionization energy, easily loses electrons) and a nonmetal (very negative electron affinity, readily gains electrons), producing oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction in a crystal lattice, not a discrete molecule. Lattice energy is the energy released when gaseous ions come together to form one mole of solid ionic compound (or equivalently, the energy needed to separate it back into gaseous ions); it follows Coulomb's law, so lattice energy increases with higher ionic charge and decreases with larger ionic radius. MgO (ions of charge +2 and -2, radii smaller than Na+ and Cl-) has a lattice energy of about 3795 kJ/mol, far higher than NaCl's 787 kJ/mol, because doubling both charges roughly quadruples the Coulombic attraction, and MgO's melting point (2852 C) is correspondingly much higher than NaCl's (801 C).

sections.heading: Covalent Bonding, Metallic Bonding, and Bond Energy
sections.body: Covalent bonds form between nonmetals sharing electron pairs in localized bonds between specific atoms, building discrete molecules (like H2O) or extended covalent networks (like diamond). Bond energy is the energy required to break one mole of a specific bond in the gas phase; a C-C single bond averages about 347 kJ/mol, a C=C double bond about 614 kJ/mol, and a C#C triple bond about 839 kJ/mol -- more shared electron pairs mean a shorter, stronger bond, though not simply double or triple the single-bond energy. Metallic bonding, described by the electron-sea model, treats metal cations as a fixed lattice bathed in a "sea" of delocalized valence electrons that belong to the crystal as a whole rather than to any one atom; this delocalization, not the electrons themselves, explains why metals conduct electricity and heat well (electrons move freely) and remain malleable and ductile (layers of cations can slide past each other without breaking discrete bonds).

lessons.workedExample: Predict the bonding in three pairs using Pauling electronegativities: Na (0.93) and F (3.98); C (2.55) and O (3.44); and Cu (1.90) with itself. Na-F: difference = 3.98 - 0.93 = 3.05, well above 1.7, so this is ionic (NaF), consistent with sodium's low ionization energy (496 kJ/mol) and fluorine's very negative electron affinity. C-O: difference = 3.44 - 2.55 = 0.89, in the polar covalent range, matching the polar C=O bonds found in CO2 and carbonyl groups. Cu-Cu: difference = 0, and since copper is a metal, this is metallic bonding via the electron-sea model, not covalent, even though the electronegativity difference alone looks like the nonpolar covalent range -- the metal/nonmetal identity of the atoms, not electronegativity difference alone, distinguishes metallic from covalent bonding.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student uses electronegativity difference correctly as a predictive tool rather than a rigid rule, and understands that metal-metal bonding is metallic regardless of the electronegativity difference being near zero. A strong answer connects lattice energy to Coulomb's law (charge and radius dependence) to explain real melting-point data, and correctly attributes metallic properties (conductivity, malleability) to electron delocalization rather than to "metal atoms being naturally soft." A weak answer applies electronegativity-difference cutoffs mechanically without checking whether the atoms involved are metals or nonmetals.

questions.prompt: MgO has a much higher lattice energy (about 3795 kJ/mol) than NaCl (about 787 kJ/mol). What best explains this difference?

options.text: Mg2+ and O2- have higher charges and smaller radii than Na+ and Cl-, both of which increase Coulombic attraction
Magnesium is a heavier element than sodium, and heavier elements always form stronger bonds
MgO is a covalent compound while NaCl is ionic, and covalent bonds are always stronger
Oxygen has a higher electronegativity than chlorine, which is the sole factor determining lattice energy

explanations.a: Correct: lattice energy follows Coulomb's law, scaling with the product of ionic charges and inversely with the distance between them; +2/-2 charges and smaller ionic radii both raise the attraction sharply compared to +1/-1 NaCl.
explanations.b: Atomic weight has no direct causal role in bond strength; the relevant variables are charge and radius, not mass.
explanations.c: MgO is an ionic compound (metal oxide with a large electronegativity difference), not covalent; the comparison here is between two ionic compounds.
explanations.d: Electronegativity difference influences bond polarity, but lattice energy specifically depends on ionic charge and radius via Coulomb's law, not electronegativity alone.

questions.prompt: Order these carbon-carbon bonds from lowest to highest average bond energy.

items.text: C-C single bond (~347 kJ/mol)
C=C double bond (~614 kJ/mol)
C#C triple bond (~839 kJ/mol)

questions.explanation: More shared electron pairs pull the bonded atoms closer and hold them more strongly, so bond energy rises from single to double to triple bonds, though not in exact integer multiples of the single-bond value.

questions.prompt: Match each bond type to the model or feature that best characterizes it.

right.text: Electrostatic attraction between ions in a crystal lattice, governed by Coulomb's law
Localized sharing of electron pairs between specific atoms
Cations in a fixed lattice surrounded by a delocalized sea of valence electrons

questions.explanation: Ionic bonding is electrostatic attraction between discrete ions (Coulomb's law sets lattice energy); covalent bonding is localized electron-pair sharing between specific atoms; metallic bonding is delocalized electrons shared across the whole lattice, explaining conductivity and malleability.

lessons.label: Molecular Geometry and VSEPR

sections.heading: Lewis Structures: Mapping Out Bonding and Lone Pairs
sections.body: A Lewis structure shows every valence electron in a molecule as either a bonding pair (shared between two atoms, drawn as a line) or a lone pair (unshared, drawn as dots) on a central atom, typically arranged so each atom (except hydrogen) reaches an octet of 8 valence electrons. Building one starts by summing all valence electrons, arranging atoms with the least electronegative nonhydrogen atom usually central, connecting atoms with single bonds, then distributing remaining electrons as lone pairs starting with terminal atoms, and finally converting lone pairs to double or triple bonds if the central atom still lacks an octet. Some molecules, like BF3 (boron has only 6 electrons) or SF6 (sulfur exceeds an octet with 12), violate the strict octet rule -- boron and other period-2 elements can be electron-deficient, while period-3-and-below elements can accommodate expanded valence shells -- traditionally attributed to d-orbital participation, though modern bonding theory instead explains this mainly through ionic character and multicenter (e.g. 3-center-4-electron) bonding.

sections.heading: VSEPR: Predicting 3D Shape from Electron Domains
sections.body: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory, developed by Ronald Gillespie and Ronald Nyholm in the 1950s-60s, predicts molecular shape from the simple premise that electron domains (bonding pairs and lone pairs alike) around a central atom arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible, minimizing repulsion. Two domains give a linear shape (180 degrees, e.g., CO2); three domains give trigonal planar (120 degrees, e.g., BF3) if all are bonds, or bent (~120 degrees, e.g., SO2) if one is a lone pair; four domains give tetrahedral (109.5 degrees, e.g., CH4) if all are bonds, trigonal pyramidal (~107 degrees, e.g., NH3) with one lone pair, or bent (~104.5 degrees, e.g., H2O) with two lone pairs. Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs because they are held by only one nucleus and spread out more, which is why NH3's bond angle (107 degrees) is compressed slightly below the ideal tetrahedral 109.5 degrees, and water's (104.5 degrees) is compressed further still by two lone pairs.

sections.heading: Hybridization and Sigma versus Pi Bonds
sections.body: Hybridization mixes an atom's atomic orbitals (s, p, sometimes d) into new hybrid orbitals matching the VSEPR electron-domain geometry: sp hybridization (2 domains, linear) mixes one s and one p orbital; sp2 (3 domains, trigonal planar) mixes one s and two p orbitals; sp3 (4 domains, tetrahedral) mixes one s and three p orbitals. A sigma (s) bond forms from head-on orbital overlap along the bond axis and is present in every single, double, and triple bond -- it is the only bond type possible in a single bond and allows free rotation. A pi (p) bond forms from sideways overlap of unhybridized p orbitals above and below the bond axis; a double bond is one sigma plus one pi bond, and a triple bond is one sigma plus two pi bonds. Pi bonds prevent rotation around the bond axis (which is why cis and trans isomers of alkenes exist) and are generally weaker per bond than sigma bonds, making double and triple bonds more reactive than single bonds.

lessons.workedExample: Determine the shape and hybridization of the central atom in ammonia, NH3. Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; three form N-H bonding pairs (3 x 2 = 6 electrons shared, nitrogen contributes 3), leaving one lone pair (2 electrons) on nitrogen, for 4 total electron domains (3 bonding + 1 lone pair). Four domains means the electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, and nitrogen is sp3 hybridized. But because one domain is a lone pair (not counted in the molecular shape, only in predicting bond angles), the observed molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal, with a measured H-N-H bond angle of about 107 degrees -- compressed from the ideal 109.5 degrees because the lone pair's greater spatial spread pushes the three N-H bonding pairs closer together.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student can distinguish electron-domain geometry (which counts lone pairs) from molecular shape (which describes only the positions of atoms), since this is the single most common VSEPR error. A strong answer correctly predicts bond-angle compression from lone pair repulsion and can identify sigma versus pi bond count in a double or triple bond. A weak answer names the electron-domain geometry when asked for molecular shape (e.g., calling water "tetrahedral" instead of "bent"), or believes a double bond is simply two identical bonds rather than one sigma and one distinct pi bond.

questions.prompt: Water, H2O, has a central oxygen atom with two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. What is its molecular shape and approximate bond angle?

options.text: Tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees
Bent, approximately 104.5 degrees
Linear, 180 degrees
Trigonal pyramidal, approximately 107 degrees

explanations.a: Tetrahedral describes the electron-domain geometry of all four domains together, but the molecular shape (positions of atoms only) is bent, and the two lone pairs compress the angle below 109.5 degrees.
explanations.b: Correct: with four total electron domains but only two atoms bonded, the molecular shape is bent; two lone pairs (which take up more space than bonding pairs) compress the H-O-H angle to about 104.5 degrees.
explanations.c: Linear would require only two electron domains with no lone pairs, or a lone-pair arrangement placing atoms 180 degrees apart, which is not the case here.
explanations.d: Trigonal pyramidal describes a central atom with three bonding pairs and one lone pair (like ammonia), not two bonding pairs and two lone pairs.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for drawing a Lewis structure in the sequence they are normally performed.

items.text: Sum all valence electrons in the molecule
Arrange atoms with single bonds connecting them
Distribute remaining electrons as lone pairs, starting with terminal atoms
Convert lone pairs to double or triple bonds if the central atom lacks an octet

questions.explanation: Lewis structures are built by first totaling valence electrons, then sketching the connectivity with single bonds, then filling out lone pairs on terminal atoms, and finally adjusting with multiple bonds only if the central atom still needs more electrons.

questions.prompt: Match each number of electron domains around a central atom (all bonding, no lone pairs) to its predicted molecular shape.

right.text: Linear, 180 degrees
Trigonal planar, 120 degrees
Tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees

questions.explanation: With no lone pairs, electron-domain geometry and molecular shape are identical: 2 domains maximize separation at 180 degrees (linear), 3 at 120 degrees (trigonal planar), and 4 at 109.5 degrees (tetrahedral).

lessons.label: Polarity and Intermolecular Forces

sections.heading: Bond Polarity versus Molecular Polarity
sections.body: Bond polarity depends only on the electronegativity difference between two bonded atoms: any difference above about 0.4 makes a bond polar covalent, with a bond dipole pointing from the less electronegative to the more electronegative atom. Molecular polarity, in contrast, depends on both bond polarities AND molecular geometry, because bond dipoles are vectors that can cancel. Carbon dioxide, O=C=O, has two very polar C=O bonds (electronegativity difference 0.89), but because the molecule is linear (VSEPR, no lone pairs on carbon), the two bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel completely, making CO2 a nonpolar molecule overall. Water, H2O, also has two polar O-H bonds, but its bent shape (104.5 degrees, from two lone pairs on oxygen) means the bond dipoles do not cancel, giving water a substantial net dipole moment of 1.85 debye.

sections.heading: Dipole Moment as a Quantitative Measure
sections.body: Dipole moment (mu) quantifies molecular polarity numerically, measured in debye units (1 D = 3.336 x 10^-30 coulomb-meters), and is calculated as charge separation multiplied by the distance between the charge centers, summed as a vector over the whole molecule. Larger electronegativity differences and geometries that do not cancel dipoles both push mu higher: HF (electronegativity difference 1.78, short bond) has mu = 1.82 D, HCl (difference 0.96, longer bond) has mu = 1.08 D, and NH3 (asymmetric trigonal pyramidal shape with a lone pair reinforcing the bond dipoles) has mu = 1.42 D. A mu of exactly zero does not mean bonds are nonpolar -- it means individual bond dipoles have cancelled by symmetry, as in CO2, CCl4, or BF3.

sections.heading: Intermolecular Forces: London Dispersion, Dipole-Dipole, and Hydrogen Bonding
sections.body: Intermolecular forces (IMFs) act between separate molecules, not within them, and are far weaker than covalent or ionic bonds, but they control physical properties like boiling point and solubility. London dispersion forces, present in ALL molecules and atoms, arise from instantaneous, temporary dipoles created by random electron motion; they grow stronger with more electrons and larger surface area, which is why nonpolar noble gases boil higher as they get larger down the group (helium boils at -269 C, xenon at -108 C, despite both being nonpolar). Dipole-dipole forces act additionally between polar molecules with permanent dipoles, aligning positive ends toward negative ends of neighboring molecules. Hydrogen bonding, the strongest common IMF (roughly 5-30 kJ/mol, versus about 1-10 kJ/mol for dispersion in similarly sized molecules), occurs specifically when hydrogen bonded to a small, highly electronegative atom (N, O, or F) is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F -- this is why water's boiling point (100 C) is anomalously high compared to H2S (-60 C), even though sulfur is larger and more polarizable, because H2S cannot hydrogen bond as effectively as water can.

lessons.workedExample: Explain why methane (CH4, boiling point -161.5 C) boils far lower than methanol (CH3OH, boiling point 64.7 C), even though the two molecules have similar molar mass (16.04 versus 32.04 g/mol -- methanol is only about double). Methane is nonpolar (tetrahedral, symmetric C-H bonds with a small electronegativity difference of 0.35 that mostly cancels), so its only IMF is weak London dispersion. Methanol has a polar O-H bond (electronegativity difference 1.24) and, critically, an O-H hydrogen directly bonded to a lone pair on a nearby oxygen, enabling hydrogen bonding between methanol molecules. Even though methanol's molar mass is only about double methane's, hydrogen bonding (roughly 20 kJ/mol per interaction) requires far more thermal energy to overcome than dispersion forces alone, explaining the 226-degree difference in boiling point.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student can separate bond polarity from molecular polarity (checking for symmetry-driven cancellation) and can correctly rank IMF strength by identifying which specific force applies to a given molecule, especially recognizing hydrogen bonding's strict N-O-F requirement. A strong answer explains an anomalous boiling point (like water versus H2S) by naming the specific IMF responsible rather than vaguely citing "polarity." A weak answer assumes any molecule with polar bonds is automatically a polar molecule, or claims all polar molecules hydrogen bond.

questions.prompt: CCl4 has four polar C-Cl bonds (electronegativity difference 0.61) but has a molecular dipole moment of zero. Why?

options.text: The tetrahedral, symmetric arrangement of the four C-Cl bond dipoles causes them to cancel as vectors
Chlorine and carbon have identical electronegativities, so the bonds are actually nonpolar
CCl4 does not actually contain any covalent bonds
Molecular dipole moment only applies to molecules containing hydrogen

explanations.a: Correct: CCl4's tetrahedral symmetry means the four individual C-Cl bond dipoles point in directions that sum to zero as vectors, even though each individual bond is polar.
explanations.b: Carbon (2.55) and chlorine (3.16) have a real electronegativity difference of 0.61, which is within the polar covalent range; the bonds themselves are polar.
explanations.c: CCl4 is held together entirely by polar covalent C-Cl bonds; it is a real, well-characterized molecule.
explanations.d: Dipole moment applies to any molecule with a geometry and bond set that produces a net charge separation; it has nothing to do with hydrogen specifically.

questions.prompt: Order these substances from lowest to highest boiling point, given their intermolecular forces: Ar (dispersion only, small), CH3OH (hydrogen bonding), HCl (dipole-dipole plus dispersion).

items.text: Ar (boiling point -186 C)
HCl (boiling point -85 C)
CH3OH (boiling point 65 C)

questions.explanation: Argon has only weak London dispersion forces and a small atomic size, giving it the lowest boiling point; HCl adds dipole-dipole attraction on top of dispersion, raising its boiling point; methanol adds hydrogen bonding, the strongest of the three IMF types present, giving it by far the highest boiling point.

questions.prompt: Match each intermolecular force to the molecule or substance where it is the dominant or defining force present.

right.text: CH4, a nonpolar tetrahedral molecule
HCl, a polar molecule with no N-H, O-H, or F-H bond
H2O, with O-H bonds and lone pairs on oxygen

questions.explanation: CH4 is nonpolar and symmetric, so only dispersion forces act between molecules; HCl is polar but lacks an N-H, O-H, or F-H bond, so it has dipole-dipole forces on top of dispersion but no hydrogen bonding; H2O has O-H bonds and lone pairs on a small, electronegative oxygen, enabling hydrogen bonding on top of dispersion and dipole-dipole forces.

lessons.label: The Mole and Avogadro Number

sections.heading: The Mole as a Counting Unit
sections.body: Chemists routinely handle numbers of atoms and molecules too large to count individually, so they use the mole the way a baker uses 'dozen' — a fixed counting unit that converts an astronomically large number of particles into a manageable lab quantity. One mole is defined as exactly 6.02214076x10^23 elementary entities, whether those entities are atoms, ions, molecules, or electrons. This number, called Avogadro's number (NA), is fixed by the 2019 redefinition of the SI base units, meaning it no longer depends on any physical measurement or artifact — it is an exact defining constant, the same way the speed of light is exact. Before 2019, the mole was defined via carbon-12: exactly 12 grams of pure carbon-12 contained one mole of atoms, and NA was measured, with tiny uncertainty, to match that definition. Today the logic runs the other way: NA is fixed by definition, and the precise mass of a mole of carbon-12 is instead what experiment now determines.

sections.heading: Avogadro's Number: History and Modern Definition
sections.body: Amedeo Avogadro never counted anything resembling 6.022x10^23 — in 1811 he simply hypothesized that equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, a bold claim with no way yet to test the actual count. The number itself was first estimated decades later, and the name 'Avogadro's number' was coined in honor of that hypothesis by French physicist Jean Perrin, who in 1909 used measurements of Brownian motion (the jittery movement of pollen-sized particles suspended in water, following Einstein's 1905 theoretical treatment) to estimate NA at roughly 6.8x10^23 — a Nobel-Prize-winning result (Physics, 1926) that gave the first solid experimental support for the atomic theory of matter. Robert Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909-1913), which measured the electron's charge, provided another route: dividing the Faraday constant (charge per mole of electrons) by the electron's charge gives NA directly. The most precise modern value came from the International Avogadro Project, which counted atoms in a nearly perfect sphere of isotopically enriched silicon-28 using X-ray crystal density (XRCD) measurements.

sections.heading: Molar Mass and the Mole Bridge
sections.body: Molar mass is the mass in grams of one mole of a substance, and it is numerically equal to the atomic mass (in amu) shown on the periodic table for elements, or the sum of atomic masses for compounds — carbon's molar mass is 12.011 g/mol, and water's is 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. For nearly all practical purposes, this equivalence is not a coincidence — it's rooted in how the atomic mass unit was originally tied to carbon-12. Since the 2019 SI redefinition fixed NA by definition, this equivalence is an extremely precise approximation rather than a mathematically exact identity, but the difference is far too small to matter for any calculation a chemist will do. Molar mass is the essential conversion factor connecting the macroscopic quantity a balance measures (grams) to the microscopic count chemists actually care about (moles of particles, and by extension, number of atoms or molecules via NA). A three-step conversion chain — grams to moles (divide by molar mass), moles to particles (multiply by NA), or the reverse — underlies nearly every quantitative calculation in chemistry, from stoichiometry to concentration to gas laws.

lessons.workedExample: A student needs to know how many individual water molecules are in a 250 mL glass of water (density 1.00 g/mL, so mass = 250 g). First, divide by water's molar mass: 250 g / 18.02 g/mol = 13.87 mol H2O. Then multiply by Avogadro's number: 13.87 mol x 6.022x10^23 molecules/mol = 8.35x10^24 molecules of water — far exceeding even the highest estimates of the number of stars in the observable universe (10^21-10^24). This two-step chain (mass to moles to particles) is the same logic used whether counting water molecules in a glass, sodium ions in a salt shaker, or reactant molecules in a beaker before a reaction — only the molar mass value changes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing the mole concept is checking whether a student treats 'mole' as a real counting unit with physical meaning, not a memorized conversion factor to plug into a formula. A weak answer says 'you divide by molar mass' without being able to explain why that operation converts grams into a particle count. A strong answer can explain that molar mass is grams per mole, so dividing grams by (grams/mole) leaves moles, and can then explain why NA is now an exact defined constant rather than a measured value — showing they understand the mole as a bridge between the atomic and macroscopic scales, not an isolated formula.

questions.prompt: As of the 2019 SI redefinition, Avogadro's number is:

options.text: An exact defined constant
A measured value with growing experimental uncertainty
An approximation that changes with temperature
Only valid for gaseous substances

explanations.a: Correct — since 2019, NA = 6.02214076x10^23 is fixed by definition, not measured.
explanations.b: Before 2019 it was a measured value; after the redefinition it became an exact constant, reversing the old relationship with the carbon-12 mass standard.
explanations.c: Avogadro's number is a fixed counting constant; it does not depend on temperature or any physical condition.
explanations.d: The mole and Avogadro's number apply to any elementary entity — atoms, ions, molecules, or electrons — not only gases.

questions.prompt: Whose Brownian-motion measurements produced the first solid experimental estimate of Avogadro's number and earned a Nobel Prize?

options.text: Amedeo Avogadro
Jean Perrin
Robert Millikan
Antoine Lavoisier

explanations.a: Avogadro only hypothesized (1811) that equal gas volumes hold equal numbers of molecules; he never measured the number itself.
explanations.b: Correct — Perrin's 1909 Brownian-motion measurements gave an experimental estimate near 6.8x10^23 and won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics.
explanations.c: Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the electron's charge, which gives NA only indirectly via the Faraday constant.
explanations.d: Lavoisier established the law of conservation of mass, unrelated to determining Avogadro's number.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in converting a measured mass of a substance into a number of particles.

items.text: Weigh the sample to find its mass in grams
Divide the mass by the molar mass to get moles
Multiply the moles by Avogadro's number
Read off the number of individual particles

questions.explanation: Mass is measured first; dividing by molar mass converts it to moles (since molar mass has units of grams per mole); multiplying moles by Avogadro's number then converts to a particle count.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its value or definition.

right.text: 6.02214076x10^23 (exact, fixed by SI definition)
Grams per mole of a substance
The SI base unit for amount of substance

questions.explanation: Avogadro's number is the fixed particle count per mole; molar mass converts grams to moles for a specific substance; the mole itself is the SI unit these two ideas connect.

lessons.label: Balancing Equations and Reaction Stoichiometry

sections.heading: Conservation of Mass and Balancing
sections.body: Antoine Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass, established through careful combustion experiments in sealed vessels during the 1770s-80s, states that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction — the same number of atoms of each element present before the reaction must be present after, just rearranged into new substances. A balanced chemical equation is the bookkeeping tool that enforces this law: coefficients are adjusted (never subscripts, which would change the identity of a compound) until the count of each element matches on both sides. For example, the unbalanced skeleton Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3 becomes balanced as 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3, giving 4 Fe atoms and 6 O atoms on each side. Balancing by inspection (trial adjustment of coefficients) works for most reactions; more complex redox reactions may require the algebraic or half-reaction method instead.

sections.heading: Reading Mole Ratios from Coefficients
sections.body: Once balanced, the coefficients in a chemical equation represent mole ratios, not mass or volume ratios — this is the single most important idea in stoichiometry. In 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3, the coefficients mean that 4 mol of iron reacts with exactly 3 mol of oxygen gas to produce 2 mol of iron(III) oxide, regardless of what mass those moles correspond to, since Fe and O2 have very different molar masses (55.85 vs 32.00 g/mol). This mole-ratio relationship is what lets a chemist predict that doubling the iron requires doubling the oxygen and doubles the product — a direct proportionality that only holds in terms of moles, never directly in grams. Every stoichiometric calculation must therefore convert into moles before using the equation's coefficients, and convert back out of moles only at the very last step.

sections.heading: Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry
sections.body: A mass-to-mass stoichiometry problem — given a mass of one substance, find the mass of another — follows a fixed three-step conversion chain: convert the given mass to moles using its molar mass, use the balanced equation's mole ratio to convert moles of the given substance to moles of the desired substance, then convert those moles to mass using the desired substance's molar mass. For 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3, finding the mass of Fe2O3 produced from 50.0 g Fe: 50.0 g Fe / 55.85 g/mol = 0.895 mol Fe; 0.895 mol Fe x (2 mol Fe2O3 / 4 mol Fe) = 0.448 mol Fe2O3; 0.448 mol x 159.7 g/mol = 71.5 g Fe2O3. Skipping the mole conversion and cross-multiplying grams directly is a very common error, since mass ratios are not the same as mole ratios unless the two substances happen to share a molar mass.

lessons.workedExample: Methane burns according to the balanced equation CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. A student wants to know how many grams of CO2 form when 16.0 g of CH4 (molar mass 16.04 g/mol) burns completely. Step 1: 16.0 g CH4 / 16.04 g/mol = 0.997 mol CH4. Step 2: using the 1:1 mole ratio of CH4 to CO2 in the balanced equation, 0.997 mol CH4 produces 0.997 mol CO2. Step 3: 0.997 mol CO2 x 44.01 g/mol = 43.9 g CO2. Notice that even though 16.0 g of methane reacts with a much larger mass of oxygen, the mole ratio — not the mass ratio — is what the coefficients directly give.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe mole-ratio reasoning because it is the fastest way to catch a student who has memorized a calculation template without understanding why it works. A weak answer plugs numbers into a formula and cannot explain why grams must first be converted to moles before using equation coefficients. A strong answer explicitly states that a balanced equation's coefficients are mole ratios, correctly identifies which two substances' coefficients to compare, and can explain what would go wrong if someone instead cross-multiplied raw masses — showing genuine grasp of conservation of mass as the reaction's underlying constraint, not just an equation-balancing exercise.

questions.prompt: In a balanced chemical equation, the coefficients directly represent ratios of:

options.text: Moles
Mass in grams
Volume for solids
Number of electrons transferred

explanations.a: Correct — balanced coefficients are mole ratios; mass and volume must be converted to moles first.
explanations.b: Mass ratios differ from mole ratios whenever the substances have different molar masses.
explanations.c: Coefficients say nothing about the volume of solids, which depends on density, not moles directly.
explanations.d: Electron transfer counts are tracked separately in redox half-reactions, not by the overall equation's coefficients.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the correctly balanced form of Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3?

options.text: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3
2Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3
4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3
4Fe + 3O2 -> 4Fe2O3

explanations.a: Unbalanced — 1 Fe and 2 O on the left do not match 2 Fe and 3 O on the right.
explanations.b: Still unbalanced — 2 Fe and 2 O on the left do not match 2 Fe and 3 O on the right.
explanations.c: Correct — 4 Fe and 6 O atoms appear on both sides, satisfying conservation of mass.
explanations.d: The Fe count is wrong: 4 Fe on the left would need 4Fe2O3 to give 8 Fe on the right, not matching.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a mass-to-mass stoichiometry calculation.

items.text: Convert the given mass to moles using its molar mass
Apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation
Convert the resulting moles to mass using the product's molar mass

questions.explanation: The equation's coefficients only relate moles, so mass must be converted into moles first, ratioed, then converted back to mass last.

questions.prompt: Match each item to its correct description.

right.text: Established the law via sealed-vessel combustion experiments in the 1770s-80s
States that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction
Shows correct mole ratios through its coefficients

questions.explanation: Lavoisier's experiments established conservation of mass, which balancing a chemical equation enforces by matching atom counts on both sides.

lessons.label: Limiting Reagents and Percent Yield

sections.heading: Identifying the Limiting Reagent
sections.body: In any real reaction where reactants are not mixed in exact stoichiometric proportions, one reactant runs out first and stops the reaction — this is the limiting reagent, and it alone determines how much product can form, no matter how much of the other reactant remains. To identify it, convert every reactant's given mass to moles, then divide each by its own coefficient in the balanced equation; whichever reactant gives the smallest quotient is limiting, because it is used up fastest relative to what the stoichiometry requires. For N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3, given 2.0 mol N2 and 3.0 mol H2: N2 gives 2.0/1 = 2.0, while H2 gives 3.0/3 = 1.0. Since 1.0 is smaller than 2.0, H2 is limiting, even though there are more moles of H2 present than N2 in absolute terms.

sections.heading: Theoretical Yield vs. Actual Yield
sections.body: Theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product that stoichiometry predicts will form, calculated entirely from the limiting reagent using the same mass-to-mass conversion chain as any stoichiometry problem — it is a ceiling, not a real lab measurement. Actual yield is what a chemist actually recovers and weighs after running the reaction, and it is almost always lower than the theoretical yield because real reactions lose product to incomplete reactions, side reactions that consume reactant without forming the desired product, mechanical losses during transfers and filtration, and impure or wet product. A synthesis with 92% actual-to-theoretical yield is generally considered excellent for a multi-step organic synthesis; introductory general-chemistry lab yields in the 60-85% range are common and are not evidence of a failed experiment, just normal experimental loss.

sections.heading: Percent Yield and the Excess Reagent
sections.body: Percent yield quantifies how efficiently a reaction actually proceeded compared to the theoretical maximum: percent yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%. A percent yield over 100% is not a triumph — it signals a measurement error, most commonly leftover unreacted starting material or solvent still present in the weighed product, inflating its mass. Meanwhile, the excess reagent is whatever reactant was not limiting; some of it is left over unreacted once the limiting reagent is consumed, and calculating exactly how much remains (grams of excess reagent originally present minus grams actually consumed in the reaction) is a standard follow-up question testing whether a student can apply the limiting-reagent mole ratio in the other direction, from limiting reagent to excess reagent instead of to product.

lessons.workedExample: A student reacts 10.0 g of Al with 20.0 g of Fe2O3 in the thermite reaction: 2Al + Fe2O3 -> Al2O3 + 2Fe. Moles: 10.0 g Al / 26.98 g/mol = 0.371 mol Al; 20.0 g Fe2O3 / 159.7 g/mol = 0.125 mol Fe2O3. Dividing by coefficients: Al gives 0.371/2 = 0.186; Fe2O3 gives 0.125/1 = 0.125. Since 0.125 is smaller, Fe2O3 is limiting. Theoretical yield of Fe: 0.125 mol Fe2O3 x (2 mol Fe / 1 mol Fe2O3) x 55.85 g/mol = 13.96 g Fe. If the student actually recovers 11.9 g Fe, percent yield = (11.9/13.96) x 100% = 85.2%, a reasonable result reflecting typical experimental losses.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about limiting reagents because it is the clearest test of whether a student can reason proportionally with two variables at once rather than mechanically applying a single mole ratio. A weak answer assumes whichever reactant has a smaller mass or fewer moles present must be limiting, without dividing by stoichiometric coefficients. A strong answer correctly divides each reactant's moles by its coefficient, explains why that comparison (not raw moles or mass) reveals the limiting reagent, and can further explain why an experimentally reported percent yield above 100% indicates a measurement problem rather than an unusually productive reaction.

questions.prompt: A reaction has 2.0 mol N2 and 3.0 mol H2 available for N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. Which reactant is limiting?

options.text: N2
H2
Neither — the amounts are exactly stoichiometric
It cannot be determined without the masses

explanations.a: N2's quotient (2.0 mol / 1) = 2.0 is larger than H2's, so N2 is the excess reagent, not the limiting one.
explanations.b: Correct — H2's quotient (3.0 mol / 3) = 1.0 is smaller than N2's 2.0, so H2 runs out first and is limiting.
explanations.c: The mole ratio needed is 1 N2 : 3 H2; having 2.0 mol N2 would require 6.0 mol H2 to be exactly stoichiometric, but only 3.0 mol H2 is present.
explanations.d: Moles alone are sufficient here — dividing each by its coefficient identifies the limiting reagent without needing mass.

questions.prompt: A student reports a percent yield of 108% for a synthesis. This most likely indicates:

options.text: An unusually efficient reaction that exceeded predictions
A measurement or purity error inflating the recovered mass
That the limiting reagent was calculated incorrectly as too large
That no product actually formed

explanations.a: Theoretical yield is a hard stoichiometric ceiling; no real reaction can exceed 100% of the mass conservation limit.
explanations.b: Correct — leftover solvent, unreacted starting material, or moisture in the weighed product commonly inflates actual yield above the true maximum.
explanations.c: An error in identifying the limiting reagent could shift the theoretical yield, but it would not itself explain a physically impossible actual-to-theoretical ratio.
explanations.d: A yield above 100% implies more mass was recovered than predicted, not that no product formed.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to identify the limiting reagent.

items.text: Convert each reactant's mass to moles
Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient in the balanced equation
Identify the reactant with the smallest quotient as limiting

questions.explanation: Moles must be found first, then normalized by dividing by each coefficient, before the smallest quotient reveals which reactant is limiting.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: The maximum product mass predicted by stoichiometry from the limiting reagent
The mass of product actually recovered and weighed in the lab
The reactant present in more than the stoichiometrically required amount

questions.explanation: Theoretical yield is a calculated maximum, actual yield is measured, and the excess reagent is whatever reactant is not limiting.

lessons.label: Empirical and Molecular Formulas

sections.heading: Percent Composition and Empirical Formula
sections.body: Percent composition expresses what fraction of a compound's total mass comes from each element, calculated as (mass of element in one mole of compound / molar mass of compound) x 100%. Working backward from experimentally measured percent composition to a formula is the empirical formula problem: assume a convenient 100 g sample, so each percentage converts directly to grams of that element; convert each element's grams to moles using its atomic molar mass; then divide every mole value by the smallest mole value in the set, which normalizes the ratios so the smallest becomes 1. If the resulting ratios are not close to whole numbers, such as 1.5 or 2.33, multiply all of them by the same small integer (2, 3, or 4) until they are — a ratio of 1.5 becomes 3 when doubled, for example.

sections.heading: From Empirical to Molecular Formula
sections.body: The empirical formula shows only the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms, but two different compounds can share the same empirical formula while having very different actual molecular formulas — CH2O is the empirical formula of both formaldehyde (molecular formula CH2O, molar mass 30.03 g/mol) and glucose (molecular formula C6H12O6, molar mass 180.16 g/mol), a six-times multiple. To find the true molecular formula, a separately measured molar mass, often from mass spectrometry or a colligative-property method like freezing-point depression, is required: divide the compound's actual molar mass by the empirical formula's mass to get a whole-number multiplier n, then multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n. For glucose, empirical formula mass = 30.03 g/mol, and 180.16 / 30.03 is approximately 6, giving molecular formula (CH2O) x 6 = C6H12O6.

sections.heading: Combustion Analysis
sections.body: Combustion analysis is the classic experimental method for determining the empirical formula of an unknown organic compound containing carbon, hydrogen, and often oxygen: a precisely weighed sample is completely burned in excess oxygen, and the CO2 and H2O produced are captured separately and weighed. Every carbon atom in the original sample ends up in a CO2 molecule, so moles of C in the sample equal moles of CO2 collected; likewise every two hydrogen atoms end up in one H2O molecule, so moles of H equal twice the moles of H2O collected. If the compound also contains oxygen, its mass cannot be measured directly this way — it is instead found by subtracting the measured masses of C and H from the original sample's total mass, since mass must be conserved.

lessons.workedExample: Combustion of a 5.00 g sample of an unknown compound containing carbon and hydrogen (and possibly oxygen) produces 15.29 g CO2 and 6.94 g H2O. Moles of C = 15.29 g / 44.01 g/mol = 0.3474 mol CO2 = 0.3474 mol C. Moles of H2O = 6.94 g / 18.02 g/mol = 0.3851 mol H2O, so moles of H = 0.3851 x 2 = 0.7702 mol H. Mass of C = 0.3474 x 12.01 = 4.172 g; mass of H = 0.7702 x 1.008 = 0.776 g; total = 4.948 g, close enough to the 5.00 g sample mass to confirm no oxygen is present. Dividing moles by the smaller value (0.3474): C = 1.00, H = 2.22; smaller multipliers (2, 3, 4, 5) leave H further from a whole number (e.g. x4 gives H = 8.88, x5 gives H = 11.1), but multiplying by 9 brings both close to whole numbers (C = 9.00, H = 19.98), giving the empirical formula C9H20, consistent with a nonane isomer.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on empirical-versus-molecular formula reasoning because it is a clean test of whether a student understands that mass-based lab data alone cannot uniquely identify a compound. A weak answer treats the empirical formula calculation as the final answer without checking whether an independently measured molar mass is needed to confirm it is also the molecular formula. A strong answer explains that infinitely many molecular formulas can share the same empirical ratio, correctly computes the multiplier n from a separate molar-mass measurement, and can explain why combustion analysis measures C and H directly but must infer oxygen by mass difference.

questions.prompt: A compound has empirical formula CH2 (empirical formula mass 14.03 g/mol) and a measured molar mass of 84.16 g/mol. What is its molecular formula?

options.text: CH2
C3H6
C6H12

explanations.a: CH2 is only the empirical formula; 84.16/14.03 is not 1, so the molecular formula must be a multiple of CH2.
explanations.b: C3H6 has a molar mass of about 42.08 g/mol, only half of the measured 84.16 g/mol.
explanations.c: Correct — 84.16/14.03 is approximately 6, giving molecular formula (CH2) x 6 = C6H12.
explanations.d: C12H24 would require a multiplier of 12, giving a molar mass near 168.3 g/mol, double the measured value.

questions.prompt: In combustion analysis, moles of hydrogen in the original sample equal:

options.text: Moles of H2O collected
Twice the moles of H2O collected
Half the moles of H2O collected
Moles of CO2 collected

explanations.a: Each H2O molecule contains two hydrogen atoms, so moles of H are double the moles of H2O, not equal to it.
explanations.b: Correct — each water molecule accounts for two hydrogen atoms from the original sample.
explanations.c: This would undercount hydrogen; the relationship doubles, rather than halves, the moles of H2O.
explanations.d: Moles of CO2 track carbon, not hydrogen, in the original sample.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding an empirical formula from percent composition data.

items.text: Assume a 100 g sample so each percentage becomes grams
Convert each element's grams to moles
Divide all mole values by the smallest mole value
Multiply by a small whole number if needed to reach whole-number ratios

questions.explanation: Assuming 100 g converts percentages to grams directly; converting to moles and normalizing by the smallest value gives the simplest ratio, which is then scaled to whole numbers if necessary.

questions.prompt: Match each compound or term to its correct formula relationship.

right.text: CH2O, multiplier n = 1
C6H12O6, multiplier n = 6
The simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound

questions.explanation: Formaldehyde and glucose both reduce to the empirical formula CH2O, differing only in the multiplier n applied to reach their actual molecular formulas.

lessons.label: Solutions, Molarity, and Dilution

sections.heading: Concentration Units: Molarity, Molality, and ppm
sections.body: Molarity (M) is the most common lab concentration unit, defined as moles of solute per liter of total solution, not solvent: M = mol solute / L solution. Molality (m) instead divides moles of solute by kilograms of solvent only: m = mol solute / kg solvent, which makes it temperature-independent (since mass, unlike volume, does not change with temperature) and is why molality, not molarity, is used in colligative-property calculations like freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation. Parts per million (ppm) is used for very dilute solutions, typically in environmental or trace-analysis contexts, and for dilute aqueous solutions near water's density is approximately 1 ppm = 1 mg solute per liter of solution, since 1 L of dilute aqueous solution has a mass close to 1000 g = 10^6 mg. Drinking-water contaminant limits, such as the EPA's 15 ppb (0.015 ppm) action level for lead, are reported in these units.

sections.heading: Preparing and Diluting a Solution
sections.body: To prepare a solution of known molarity from a solid solute, a chemist calculates the required mass (moles needed x molar mass), weighs it precisely on an analytical balance, dissolves it in less than the final volume of solvent (dissolving in the full volume risks overshooting, since dissolved solute and solvent do not always occupy strictly additive volumes), then transfers it to a volumetric flask and adds solvent up to the calibration mark exactly — this last step, called diluting to volume, is what makes the final concentration precisely known. Diluting an existing stock solution to a lower concentration uses the relationship M1V1 = M2V2, where M1V1 is the moles of solute in the concentrated stock (unchanged by dilution) and M2V2 is that same amount of moles now spread through a larger final volume V2.

sections.heading: Solution Stoichiometry
sections.body: Solution stoichiometry extends ordinary mass-to-mass stoichiometry to reactions run in aqueous solution: since molarity times volume gives moles directly (moles = molarity x liters), a known volume and molarity of one reactant substitutes for a measured mass as the starting point of a stoichiometric calculation. This is the basis of titration, where a solution of precisely known concentration (the titrant) is added from a buret until a reaction with an unknown-concentration solution reaches its equivalence point, often signaled by a color-change indicator, and the titrant's volume at that point is used with mole-ratio reasoning to calculate the unknown solution's exact concentration.

lessons.workedExample: A chemist has 250 mL of 6.00 M HCl stock solution and needs 100 mL of 1.50 M HCl for an experiment. Using M1V1 = M2V2: (6.00 M)(V1) = (1.50 M)(100 mL), so V1 = (1.50 x 100) / 6.00 = 25.0 mL. The chemist measures exactly 25.0 mL of the 6.00 M stock using a pipet, transfers it to a 100 mL volumetric flask, and adds water up to the calibration mark, yielding exactly 100 mL of 1.50 M HCl. Only 25.0 mL of the original 250 mL stock was needed — the remaining 225 mL stays available at its original 6.00 M concentration for other dilutions.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges test dilution reasoning because M1V1 = M2V2 is frequently applied as a memorized formula without understanding why it works — it holds because moles of solute (M times V) are conserved during dilution, and only the volume of solvent changes. A weak answer plugs numbers into the formula without being able to state what stays constant during a dilution. A strong answer explicitly states that moles of solute are unchanged, correctly identifies which given values are M1, V1, M2, and V2, and can explain why molality rather than molarity is preferred when temperature will vary during an experiment.

questions.prompt: Which concentration unit is defined using kilograms of solvent rather than liters of solution, making it temperature-independent?

options.text: Molarity
Molality
Parts per million
Percent by volume

explanations.a: Molarity uses liters of solution, which expands slightly with temperature, making molarity temperature-dependent.
explanations.b: Correct — molality divides by kilograms of solvent, a mass that does not change with temperature.
explanations.c: Parts per million is typically expressed relative to solution mass or volume, not defined around temperature independence.
explanations.d: Percent by volume compares volumes of solute and solution, which also shift with temperature.

questions.prompt: A stock solution of 12.0 M HCl is diluted to prepare 500 mL of 0.500 M HCl. What volume of the stock solution is needed?

explanations.b: 12.0 mL does not satisfy M1V1 = M2V2 for the given concentrations and final volume.
explanations.c: 41.6 mL is double the correct volume, as if M1 had been mistakenly halved to 6.00 M.
explanations.d: 6.00 mL is too small and does not solve the M1V1 = M2V2 relationship correctly.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to prepare a solution of known molarity from a solid solute.

items.text: Calculate the mass needed from moles required and molar mass
Weigh the solute on an analytical balance
Dissolve the solute in less than the final volume of solvent
Transfer to a volumetric flask and add solvent to the calibration mark

questions.explanation: The required mass is calculated first, then weighed, dissolved in a partial volume, and finally diluted to the exact calibrated volume.

questions.prompt: Match each concentration unit to its defining ratio.

right.text: mol solute / L solution
mol solute / kg solvent
mg solute / L solution

questions.explanation: Molarity uses solution volume, molality uses solvent mass, and dilute aqueous ppm approximates to mg solute per liter of solution.

lessons.label: Gases and the Ideal Gas Law

sections.heading: The Ideal Gas Law: PV = nRT
sections.body: The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, unifies Boyle's law (P and V inversely related at constant n and T), Charles's law (V and T directly related at constant n and P), and Avogadro's law (V and n directly related at constant P and T) into a single equation relating pressure (P), volume (V), moles (n), and absolute temperature (T, always in kelvin) through the gas constant R. R takes different numerical values depending on the units used: 0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K) when pressure is in atmospheres and volume in liters, or 8.314 J/(mol*K) when working in SI units of pascals and cubic meters — using the wrong R for the given units is one of the most common gas-law errors.

sections.heading: Molar Volume at STP
sections.body: At Standard Temperature and Pressure, one mole of any ideal gas occupies the same volume, since PV = nRT rearranges to V = nRT/P and n, R, T, P are all fixed. Using the traditional STP definition still taught in most US general-chemistry courses — 0 degrees C (273.15 K) and 1 atm — that volume is 22.4 L/mol. IUPAC's current official STP definition instead uses 100 kPa, slightly below 1 atm's 101.325 kPa, which gives a molar volume of 22.7 L/mol; students should check which convention a given problem or exam is using, since the two values are close but not interchangeable. Molar volume lets gas volume substitute directly for moles in stoichiometry without needing the full ideal gas law.

sections.heading: Gas Stoichiometry and Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
sections.body: Gas stoichiometry uses molar volume at STP, or the ideal gas law directly at non-standard conditions, to convert between the volume of a gaseous reactant or product and moles, exactly the way molar mass converts between grams and moles — the balanced equation's mole ratios then connect any two substances in the reaction, gas or otherwise. When multiple gases share a container, John Dalton's law of partial pressures, presented in an 1801 lecture series and published in 1802, states that the total pressure equals the sum of each individual gas's partial pressure: Ptotal = P1 + P2 + P3 + ..., and each gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times the total pressure (Pi = Xi x Ptotal) — the basis for correcting collected-gas volumes for water vapor pressure when a gas is collected over water.

sections.heading: Where Real Gases Deviate
sections.body: The ideal gas law assumes gas particles have zero volume and no intermolecular attractions or repulsions, an approximation that breaks down at high pressure, where particles are forced close enough together that their actual volume becomes a significant fraction of the container volume, and at low temperature, where particles move slowly enough for intermolecular attractive forces to measurably pull them together, reducing the pressure they exert. The van der Waals equation, (P + an^2/V^2)(V - nb) = nRT, corrects for both effects: the a term accounts for intermolecular attraction, and the b term accounts for the finite volume of gas particles themselves; gases with strong attractive forces, like NH3, or larger molecular size deviate more than small nonpolar gases like He or H2.

lessons.workedExample: A student collects 250 mL of H2 gas over water at 25 degrees C (298 K) and 762 mmHg total pressure. Water's vapor pressure at 25 degrees C is about 23.8 mmHg, so by Dalton's law the partial pressure of dry H2 is 762 - 23.8 = 738.2 mmHg = 0.9713 atm. Using PV = nRT: n = PV/(RT) = (0.9713 atm x 0.250 L) / (0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K) x 298 K) = 0.00993 mol H2. Without correcting for water vapor pressure, the student would overestimate the moles of dry H2 collected, since some of that 250 mL of gas volume is actually water vapor, not hydrogen — a routine correction whenever a gas is collected by water displacement.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe gas-collection-over-water problems because they combine two ideas at once, the ideal gas law and Dalton's law, and expose whether a student mechanically plugs total pressure into PV = nRT or actually accounts for water vapor's contribution. A weak answer uses the measured total pressure directly, silently overcounting the gas of interest. A strong answer correctly subtracts the water vapor pressure at the given temperature before solving for moles, can state why R's value must match the pressure and volume units used, and recognizes when a problem intends 22.4 versus 22.7 L/mol depending on which STP convention it specifies.

questions.prompt: Which value of R should be used when pressure is given in atmospheres and volume in liters?

options.text: 0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K)
1.00 atm

explanations.a: 8.314 J/(mol*K) is correct only when pressure is in pascals and volume in cubic meters, not atm and liters.
explanations.b: Correct — 0.08206 L*atm/(mol*K) matches units of atmospheres and liters directly.
explanations.c: That value is Avogadro's number, unrelated to the gas constant.
explanations.d: 1.00 atm is a pressure value, not the gas constant R.

questions.prompt: When a gas is collected over water, to find the moles of dry gas collected a student must first:

options.text: Ignore water vapor pressure entirely
Subtract water's vapor pressure at that temperature from the total measured pressure
Add water's vapor pressure to the total measured pressure
Divide the total pressure by 2

explanations.a: Ignoring water vapor pressure overestimates the moles of the dry gas of interest.
explanations.b: Correct — Dalton's law means the dry gas's partial pressure is the total pressure minus water's vapor pressure at that temperature.
explanations.c: Adding, rather than subtracting, water's vapor pressure would overcorrect and understate the dry gas's partial pressure.
explanations.d: There is no reason to divide by 2; the correction is a subtraction based on Dalton's law, not a halving.

questions.prompt: Real gases deviate most from ideal behavior under which conditions?

options.text: Low pressure and high temperature
High pressure and low temperature
High pressure and high temperature
Low pressure and low temperature

explanations.a: Low pressure and high temperature are exactly the conditions where real gases behave most ideally, not least.
explanations.b: Correct — high pressure packs molecules closer (finite volume matters) and low temperature slows them enough for intermolecular attraction to matter.
explanations.c: High temperature counteracts the deviation caused by high pressure, since fast-moving particles are less affected by attractive forces.
explanations.d: Low pressure keeps particles far apart, minimizing both volume and attraction effects even at low temperature.

questions.prompt: Order the historical development of gas-law understanding.

items.text: Boyle's law relates pressure and volume at constant moles and temperature
Charles's and Avogadro's laws add temperature and mole dependence
The individual gas laws are combined into PV = nRT
The van der Waals equation corrects PV = nRT for real-gas behavior

questions.explanation: Boyle's law came first, followed by laws adding temperature and mole dependence, which were unified into the ideal gas law, later corrected for real-gas deviations by van der Waals.

questions.prompt: Match each law or quantity to its statement or value.

left.text: Molar volume at STP (1 atm, 0 degrees C convention)

right.text: Total pressure equals the sum of partial pressures
22.4 L/mol
Corrects the ideal gas law for particle volume and intermolecular attraction

questions.explanation: Dalton's law sums partial pressures, the traditional STP convention gives 22.4 L/mol, and van der Waals adds real-gas correction terms to PV = nRT.

lessons.label: Classifying Chemical Reactions

sections.heading: Five patterns, one goal: predict the products
sections.body: Most introductory reactions fall into a handful of recognizable patterns, and naming the pattern is really a shortcut for predicting what comes out the other side. Synthesis (combination) reactions take two or more simple substances and combine them into one: A + B -> AB, as in N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. Decomposition runs the pattern backward, AB -> A + B, as when hydrogen peroxide breaks down, 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2, a reaction fast enough to fizz visibly once catalyzed by MnO2 or the enzyme catalase. Single displacement (A + BC -> AC + B) swaps one element into a compound, displacing another, as in Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Double displacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB) swaps partners between two ionic compounds, usually driven by a precipitate, gas, or water forming. Combustion is a hydrocarbon or organic fuel reacting with O2 to give CO2 and H2O (complete) or CO and soot (incomplete).

sections.heading: The Haber-Bosch synthesis as a case study
sections.body: The industrial synthesis of ammonia, N2 + 3H2 <-> 2NH3, is the textbook synthesis reaction, and its history shows why classification matters beyond a worksheet.
