sections.heading: Endothermic vs exothermic; calorimetry
sections.body: A reaction is EXOTHERMIC if it releases heat to the surroundings (delta-H negative — think combustion, releasing roughly 890 kJ/mol for methane) and ENDOTHERMIC if it absorbs heat (delta-H positive — dissolving ammonium nitrate in water, used in instant cold packs, absorbs about 25.7 kJ/mol). Calorimetry measures these heats experimentally: a coffee-cup calorimeter (two nested styrofoam cups, a lid, and a thermometer) approximates constant pressure and gives delta-H directly from q = mc(delta-T) for the solution, assuming the reaction's heat all goes into warming or cooling the surrounding water. A bomb calorimeter instead seals the reaction in a rigid steel vessel submerged in water, so no volume change is possible (constant volume), and it measures delta-U rather than delta-H — the two differ by the delta(ngas)RT correction term, which matters most for reactions that change the moles of gas.

lessons.workedExample: A student burns 1.00 g of ethanol in a coffee-cup calorimeter containing 200.0 g of water, and the water temperature rises from 22.0 C to 34.6 C. Using q = mc(delta-T) with water's specific heat 4.184 J/(g C): q = (200.0 g)(4.184 J/g C)(12.6 C) = 10,544 J released to the water, so the reaction released about 10.544 kJ per gram of ethanol burned. Ethanol's molar mass is 46.07 g/mol, so the measured molar enthalpy of combustion is roughly -10.544 kJ/g x 46.07 g/mol = -485.8 kJ/mol per this crude coffee-cup setup — noticeably less negative than the accepted bomb-calorimeter value near -1367 kJ/mol, because an open cup loses heat to the air and doesn't fully capture combustion's high-temperature flame energy.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes whether a student can distinguish what they MEASURED (a temperature change in a fixed mass of water) from what they REPORT (a molar enthalpy), and whether they can explain the gap between a rough classroom coffee-cup value and a literature bomb-calorimeter value rather than treating the discrepancy as a mystery. A strong answer names specific heat losses (open cup, incomplete combustion, heat capacity of the cup itself) as the cause; a weak answer either ignores the mismatch or blames it vaguely on 'human error' without a specific mechanism.

questions.prompt: Under the IUPAC sign convention used in delta-U = q + w, if a gas inside a system expands and pushes back the surroundings, the work term w for the system is:

options.text: Positive, because the system gained energy
Negative, because the system did work on the surroundings
Zero, because work only matters at constant volume
Undefined until temperature is known

explanations.a: Expansion work is energy leaving the system to push back the surroundings, not energy gained.
explanations.b: Correct — in the IUPAC convention w is work done ON the system, so a system doing expansion work on its surroundings has negative w.
explanations.c: Work is exactly zero only for a rigid, constant-volume container; a gas expanding against pressure does nonzero work.
explanations.d: The sign of w is determined by the direction of energy transfer, not by temperature alone.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists usually track delta-H rather than delta-U for reactions run in an open beaker on a lab bench?

options.text: Delta-H and delta-U are always numerically identical
At constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals delta-H directly, matching the open, atmosphere-exposed lab setup
Delta-U cannot be measured under any conditions
Delta-H is a path function while delta-U is not

explanations.a: They are equal only when a reaction produces no change in moles of gas; otherwise they differ by a pressure-volume work term.
explanations.b: Correct — q_p = delta-H at constant pressure, and an open beaker is essentially a constant-pressure system.
explanations.c: Delta-U is measurable; a bomb calorimeter measures it directly under constant-volume conditions.
explanations.d: Both delta-H and delta-U are state functions; heat and work, not enthalpy or internal energy, are the path-dependent quantities.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for finding a molar enthalpy of combustion from coffee-cup calorimeter data.

items.text: Record the water's temperature change, delta-T
Compute heat absorbed by the water: q = mc(delta-T)
Divide q by the moles of fuel burned to get molar enthalpy

questions.explanation: You must first measure the temperature change, then convert it to a heat quantity using specific heat and mass, and only then normalize that heat per mole of fuel to report a molar enthalpy.

questions.prompt: Match each calorimeter type to the quantity it directly measures.

right.text: delta-H
delta-U

questions.explanation: A coffee-cup calorimeter is open to atmospheric pressure, so its measured heat equals delta-H; a sealed bomb calorimeter holds volume constant, so no pressure-volume work occurs and its measured heat equals delta-U.

lessons.label: Enthalpy and Hess's Law

sections.heading: Enthalpy of reaction and of formation
sections.body: The standard enthalpy of reaction, delta-H-rxn-standard, is the heat released or absorbed when reactants convert fully to products at standard conditions (1 bar, and typically 298 K, with all species in their standard states). The STANDARD ENTHALPY OF FORMATION, delta-Hf-standard, is a special case: the enthalpy change for forming exactly one mole of a compound from its elements in their standard states — by definition, delta-Hf-standard for any element in its standard state (O2 gas, graphite, N2 gas) is exactly zero, giving every other compound a value relative to that zero point. These tabulated formation values, published extensively in NIST and CODATA compilations, let chemists predict a reaction's enthalpy without ever running it: water's delta-Hf-standard is -285.8 kJ/mol (liquid) versus -241.8 kJ/mol (gas), a roughly 44 kJ/mol gap that is exactly the heat of vaporization, illustrating that enthalpy of formation depends on the physical state specified.

sections.heading: Hess's law
sections.body: In 1840, Swiss-Russian chemist Germain Hess published what became known as Hess's law (the law of constant heat summation): because enthalpy is a state function, the total delta-H for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or a sequence of steps, so delta-H-rxn can be built algebraically from delta-Hf-standard values as delta-H-rxn = sigma(delta-Hf-standard, products) minus sigma(delta-Hf-standard, reactants), each weighted by its stoichiometric coefficient. Hess arrived at this before atomic theory or thermodynamics were fully formalized, from careful calorimetric measurements on multi-step reaction sequences that always summed to the same total heat regardless of route. This is the single most-used tool in thermochemistry: it means no one has to calorimetrically measure every possible reaction, since any reaction's enthalpy can be reconstructed by adding and subtracting known formation or combustion data, reversing steps (which flips delta-H's sign) and scaling steps (which scales delta-H proportionally).

sections.heading: Bond enthalpies
sections.body: An alternative, cruder route to delta-H-rxn uses average BOND ENTHALPIES — the average energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond type across many different molecules (C-H bonds average about 413 kJ/mol, O=O about 498 kJ/mol, N-triple-bond-N about 945 kJ/mol, reflecting nitrogen's exceptionally strong triple bond and explaining why N2 is so unreactive). Because breaking bonds always requires energy input (endothermic) and forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic), delta-H-rxn is approximated as sigma(bonds broken in reactants) minus sigma(bonds formed in products). This method is less accurate than tabulated formation enthalpies because bond enthalpies are AVERAGES across many different molecular environments — a C-H bond in methane is not identical to a C-H bond in benzene — so bond-enthalpy estimates typically carry larger uncertainty, useful for quick estimates but not for precise thermochemical work.

lessons.workedExample: Find delta-H-rxn for CH4(g) + 2O2(g) to CO2(g) + 2H2O(l), given delta-Hf-standard: CH4 = -74.8 kJ/mol, CO2 = -393.5 kJ/mol, H2O(l) = -285.8 kJ/mol, and O2 = 0 kJ/mol (element in standard state). Products sum: (-393.5) + 2(-285.8) = -965.1 kJ. Reactants sum: (-74.8) + 2(0) = -74.8 kJ. Delta-H-rxn = -965.1 - (-74.8) = -890.3 kJ/mol, matching the commonly cited value for methane combustion and confirming why natural gas heating releases roughly 890 kJ per mole (about 55.6 kJ per gram) of methane burned.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge cares whether a student can apply Hess's law algebraically rather than just recite it — flipping the sign of a reversed reaction, scaling delta-H when a step is doubled, and correctly subtracting reactant sums from product sums rather than the reverse. A strong answer shows the arithmetic explicitly and can explain WHY delta-Hf-standard of an element is defined as zero; a weak answer gets the products-minus-reactants order backward or cannot say what makes a substance's standard state 'standard' in the first place.

questions.prompt: By definition, the standard enthalpy of formation of O2(g) at 298 K and 1 bar is:

options.text: -393.5 kJ/mol
Exactly zero, because it is an element in its standard state
+498 kJ/mol, equal to its bond enthalpy
Undefined, because O2 is not a compound

explanations.a: That value is the formation enthalpy of CO2, not O2.
explanations.b: Correct — every element in its standard state is defined to have delta-Hf-standard equal to zero, which is what makes formation enthalpies a usable relative scale.
explanations.c: Bond enthalpy is a different quantity (the energy to break the O=O bond), not the formation enthalpy of O2 itself.
explanations.d: Formation enthalpy is defined for elements too; it is simply set to zero for them by convention.

questions.prompt: Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that:

options.text: Heat is a state function
Enthalpy is a state function, so total delta-H is path-independent
All reactions are exothermic
Work done by a system is always zero

explanations.a: Heat itself is a path function, not a state function; it is enthalpy (H), not heat, whose state-function property underlies Hess's law.
explanations.b: Correct — because H is a state function, the sum of delta-H over any sequence of steps connecting the same start and end points is fixed, which is exactly Hess's law.
explanations.c: Many reactions are endothermic; Hess's law applies equally to both signs of delta-H.
explanations.d: Work is frequently nonzero, especially in reactions with gas-volume changes; that fact is unrelated to Hess's law.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to compute delta-H-rxn from tabulated formation enthalpies.

items.text: Look up delta-Hf-standard for every reactant and product
Multiply each value by its stoichiometric coefficient and sum separately for products and reactants
Subtract the reactant sum from the product sum

questions.explanation: You need the raw formation values first, then weight and sum them by stoichiometry on each side, and only then take the products-minus-reactants difference to get delta-H-rxn.

questions.prompt: Match each thermochemical concept to its correct description.

right.text: Uses molecule-specific tabulated data; generally more accurate
Uses averaged bond energies across many molecules; a rougher estimate

questions.explanation: Formation-enthalpy Hess's-law calculations use precisely measured, substance-specific values, while bond-enthalpy estimates average over many chemical environments and so carry more uncertainty.

lessons.label: Entropy and the Second Law

sections.heading: Entropy as the dispersal of energy and matter
sections.body: German physicist Rudolf Clausius coined the term ENTROPY in 1865 (from the Greek for 'transformation'), defining delta-S = q-reversible / T for a reversible process. Ludwig Boltzmann later gave entropy a molecular meaning with S = k ln(W), where W is the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates) consistent with a system's macroscopic state and k is Boltzmann's constant, 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K — a relationship so central that it is carved on Boltzmann's tombstone in Vienna. Modern chemistry teaching frames entropy less as 'disorder' (a loose, sometimes misleading analogy) and more precisely as the DISPERSAL of energy and matter among available microstates: a gas has far higher entropy than a solid not because it is 'messier' but because its molecules can occupy vastly more possible position-and-momentum combinations at a given energy.

sections.heading: Predicting the sign of delta-S
sections.body: Several reliable patterns predict whether a process increases or decreases entropy. Entropy increases going solid to liquid to gas (more microstates available as molecular freedom increases); it increases when the number of moles of gas increases in a reaction (more independent gas particles to arrange); it increases when a solid or liquid dissolves into solution (though dissolving ions in water can locally decrease solvent entropy through hydration shells, complicating simple predictions); and it increases with increasing temperature at fixed phase, since more vibrational and translational energy states become accessible. For 2 NH3(g) to N2(g) + 3H2(g), moles of gas go from 2 to 4, so delta-S is positive; this reaction's actual delta-S-standard is +198.1 J/(mol K), consistent with the mole-of-gas-increase heuristic.

sections.heading: The second law and standard entropies
sections.body: The SECOND LAW OF THERMODYNAMICS states that for any spontaneous process, the total entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings) must increase: delta-S-universe = delta-S-system + delta-S-surroundings > 0. This resolves an apparent paradox — many spontaneous processes (water freezing, a gas compressing) DECREASE the system's own entropy — because they release enough heat to the surroundings to more than compensate, keeping the universe's total entropy climbing. Unlike delta-Hf-standard, standard molar entropies (S-standard) are NOT zero for elements; the third law instead sets S equal to zero only for a perfect crystal at absolute zero, so every substance, including elements, has a positive tabulated S-standard value at 298 K — graphite is 5.74 J/(mol K) while diamond, more rigidly ordered, is only 2.38 J/(mol K), a textbook illustration of structural order suppressing microstate count.

lessons.workedExample: Predict and then check the sign of delta-S for CaCO3(s) to CaO(s) + CO2(g) using standard entropies S-standard: CaCO3 = 91.7 J/(mol K), CaO = 38.1 J/(mol K), CO2 = 213.8 J/(mol K). Prediction: a gas is produced from two solids, so delta-S should be strongly positive. Calculation: delta-S-rxn = [38.1 + 213.8] - [91.7] = 251.9 - 91.7 = +160.2 J/(mol K). The large positive value confirms the heuristic and explains why limestone calcination (this exact reaction, used to produce lime for cement) becomes thermodynamically favorable at high temperature despite being endothermic — the TdeltaS term eventually dominates delta-H as temperature rises.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes entropy reasoning because it is the concept students most often get sloppily 'disorder'-flavored about; a strong answer explicitly reasons from moles of gas, phase, and microstate count, and correctly separates system entropy from universe entropy when explaining a spontaneous exothermic process that lowers the system's own entropy. A weak answer says something increases entropy because it 'looks messier' without connecting that to a measurable driver like gas moles or temperature, or claims a spontaneous process must increase the SYSTEM's entropy (true only when the surroundings' contribution is ignored).

questions.prompt: According to the second law of thermodynamics, a spontaneous process must:

options.text: Always increase the entropy of the system
Always increase the total entropy of the universe (system plus surroundings)
Always be exothermic
Always decrease the entropy of the surroundings

explanations.a: Many spontaneous processes, like water freezing below 0 C, decrease the system's own entropy.
explanations.b: Correct — the second law requires delta-S-universe > 0, even when the system's entropy alone decreases, as long as the surroundings gain more.
explanations.c: Spontaneous processes can be endothermic, such as ice melting above 0 C, as long as delta-S-universe is positive overall.
explanations.d: The surroundings' entropy change can be positive or negative; only the universe total is constrained to increase.

questions.prompt: Diamond has a lower standard molar entropy (2.38 J/mol K) than graphite (5.74 J/mol K) primarily because:

options.text: Diamond is an element and graphite is not
Diamond's rigid, highly ordered 3-D bonded structure allows fewer accessible microstates than graphite's layered structure
Diamond has a negative standard enthalpy of formation
Third-law entropy does not apply to carbon allotropes

explanations.a: Both diamond and graphite are elemental carbon; the difference is structural, not elemental identity.
explanations.b: Correct — diamond's tightly bonded lattice restricts atomic arrangement and vibrational freedom far more than graphite's looser layered sheets, giving it fewer accessible microstates and lower entropy.
explanations.c: Formation enthalpy is a separate quantity from standard entropy and does not explain the entropy difference here.
explanations.d: The third law applies to every substance, including both carbon allotropes; it is exactly what allows S-standard to be tabulated for each.

questions.prompt: Order these substances from lowest to highest expected standard molar entropy at the same temperature.

items.text: A perfect crystalline solid
A liquid
A gas

questions.explanation: Entropy rises from solid to liquid to gas because each phase transition grants molecules access to a larger number of positional and momentum microstates.

questions.prompt: Match each scientist to their contribution to entropy theory.

right.text: Coined 'entropy' and defined delta-S = q-reversible / T (1865)
Defined S = k ln(W), linking entropy to microstate count

questions.explanation: Clausius introduced the macroscopic thermodynamic definition of entropy, while Boltzmann later supplied its statistical-mechanical, microstate-counting interpretation.

lessons.label: Gibbs Free Energy and Spontaneity

sections.heading: Delta-G = delta-H minus T delta-S
sections.body: American physicist Josiah Willard Gibbs, in his monumental 1876-1878 paper 'On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances,' defined a quantity now called Gibbs free energy: G = H - TS. At constant temperature and pressure, delta-G = delta-H - T(delta-S) combines the first law's energy bookkeeping (delta-H) with the second law's entropy requirement (delta-S) into a single system-only quantity, so chemists no longer need to separately track the surroundings' entropy change to judge spontaneity. This is possible because delta-S-surroundings, for a process at constant T and P, equals -delta-H-system / T (heat leaving the system enters the surroundings and vice versa); substituting that into delta-S-universe = delta-S-system + delta-S-surroundings and multiplying through by -T reproduces exactly delta-G = delta-H - T(delta-S), linking Gibbs's system-level formula back to the second law's universe-level requirement.

sections.heading: Spontaneity criteria and temperature dependence
sections.body: A process is spontaneous (thermodynamically favorable, though not necessarily fast) when delta-G is negative, at equilibrium when delta-G equals zero, and nonspontaneous as written when delta-G is positive. Because delta-G = delta-H - T(delta-S), the temperature dependence splits into four cases: delta-H negative and delta-S positive gives delta-G negative at ALL temperatures (always spontaneous); delta-H positive and delta-S negative gives delta-G positive at all temperatures (never spontaneous); delta-H negative and delta-S negative is spontaneous only at LOW temperature (the -T delta-S term stays small); and delta-H positive and delta-S positive is spontaneous only at HIGH temperature (the -T delta-S term eventually outweighs delta-H). Ice melting (delta-H positive, delta-S positive) is the textbook case of the fourth pattern, spontaneous only above 0 C at 1 atm.

sections.heading: Delta-G-standard and the equilibrium constant K
sections.body: Gibbs free energy connects directly to chemical equilibrium through delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K), where R is 8.314 J/(mol K) and K is the equilibrium constant at temperature T. A large K (products favored) corresponds to a strongly negative delta-G-standard; a small K (reactants favored) corresponds to a positive delta-G-standard; K equal to exactly 1 corresponds to delta-G-standard equal to zero. This single equation is why thermodynamic tables of delta-Gf-standard let chemists PREDICT equilibrium constants for reactions that have never been run — a use central to industrial process design, such as estimating how far the Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis (delta-G-standard around -33 kJ/mol at 298 K) shifts toward products before temperature is raised for kinetic reasons, trading equilibrium favorability for reaction rate.

lessons.workedExample: For the reaction N2(g) + 3H2(g) to 2NH3(g) at 298 K, delta-H-standard = -92.2 kJ/mol and delta-S-standard = -198.1 J/(mol K). Compute delta-G-standard: delta-G = -92,200 J/mol - (298 K)(-198.1 J/mol K) = -92,200 + 59,033.8 = -33,166.2 J/mol, or about -33.2 kJ/mol, confirming the reaction is spontaneous at 298 K despite its unfavorable (negative) entropy change, because the strongly negative delta-H dominates at room temperature. Using delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K): ln(K) = 33,166.2 / (8.314 x 298) = 13.39, so K is approximately e^13.39, on the order of 6 x 10^5 — a large equilibrium constant, meaning ammonia is strongly favored at equilibrium at 298 K, even though industrially the Haber process runs at 400-500 C for faster kinetics, which actually lowers K in exchange for usable reaction rate.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge asks about delta-G's temperature dependence because it is the single concept students most often flatten into 'negative delta-G means spontaneous, full stop,' missing that spontaneity can flip with temperature when delta-H and delta-S have the same sign. A strong answer identifies which of the four sign-combination cases a reaction falls into and states the temperature behavior that follows; a weak answer plugs numbers into delta-G = delta-H - T delta-S without being able to say why the sign of that answer could reverse at a different temperature.

questions.prompt: A reaction has delta-H-standard positive and delta-S-standard positive. Under what temperature condition is it spontaneous?

options.text: Only at low temperature
Only at high temperature
At all temperatures
At no temperature

explanations.a: At low temperature the -T delta-S term is small, leaving the positive delta-H dominant, so the reaction is nonspontaneous.
explanations.b: Correct — as T rises, the -T delta-S term (delta-S positive, so this term is negative and growing in magnitude) eventually outweighs the positive delta-H, making delta-G negative.
explanations.c: It cannot be spontaneous at all temperatures because delta-H is positive and dominates at low T.
explanations.d: It IS spontaneous at sufficiently high temperature, so 'never' is incorrect.

questions.prompt: If delta-G-standard for a reaction is a large positive number, the equilibrium constant K is:

options.text: Much greater than 1
Exactly 1
Much less than 1
Undefined

explanations.a: A K much greater than 1 corresponds to a strongly negative, not positive, delta-G-standard.
explanations.b: K equal to 1 corresponds to delta-G-standard equal to zero, not a large positive value.
explanations.c: Correct — from delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K), a large positive delta-G-standard forces ln(K) to be a large negative number, so K is much less than 1 (reactants favored).
explanations.d: K is well-defined for any finite delta-G-standard via the same equation; it is simply small in this case.

questions.prompt: Order these steps to estimate an equilibrium constant K from tabulated thermodynamic data.

items.text: Look up or calculate delta-H-standard and delta-S-standard for the reaction
Compute delta-G-standard = delta-H-standard - T(delta-S-standard) at the temperature of interest
Solve delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K) for K

questions.explanation: You need delta-H and delta-S first to build delta-G-standard at a chosen temperature, and only once delta-G-standard is known can you solve for K via delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K).

questions.prompt: Match each delta-G-standard value to what it implies about K.

right.text: K much greater than 1

questions.explanation: Delta-G-standard = -RT ln(K) means delta-G-standard = 0 forces ln(K) = 0, so K = 1, while a strongly negative delta-G-standard forces a large positive ln(K), giving K much greater than 1.

lessons.label: Heating/Cooling Curves and Phase Changes

sections.heading: Phase transitions and latent heat
sections.body: During a phase change (melting, freezing, boiling, condensing), a substance absorbs or releases energy WITHOUT changing temperature, because that energy is going entirely into breaking or forming intermolecular attractions rather than increasing average kinetic energy. This energy per mole (or per gram) is called LATENT HEAT: the latent heat of fusion (solid-liquid) for water is 6.01 kJ/mol (334 J/g), and the latent heat of vaporization (liquid-gas) is about 40.7 kJ/mol (2260 J/g) at 100 C and 1 atm. Vaporization requires roughly 6-7 times more energy than fusion for water because boiling must fully separate molecules against essentially all of their intermolecular attraction (mostly hydrogen bonding), whereas melting only needs to disrupt the rigid, ordered lattice structure while molecules stay in close contact — this large gap is why steam burns are so much more dangerous than equivalent-temperature hot water.

sections.heading: Specific heat and q = mc(delta-T)
sections.body: Within a single phase (no transition happening), added heat DOES raise temperature, governed by q = mc(delta-T), where c is the substance's specific heat capacity — the energy needed to raise one gram by one degree Celsius. Water's specific heat, 4.184 J/(g C), is unusually high compared to most substances (metals typically run 0.1-0.9 J/g C) because of extensive hydrogen bonding, which is why large bodies of water moderate coastal climates and why water is used as a coolant. Water's specific heat also differs by phase: liquid water is 4.184 J/(g C), ice is about 2.09 J/(g C), and steam is about 2.0 J/(g C) — roughly half the liquid value in both other phases, meaning a heating curve's slope is steeper (temperature rises faster per joule) in the solid and gas regions than in the liquid region.

sections.heading: Interpreting a heating curve
sections.body: A full heating curve for a pure substance, plotting temperature against heat added at constant pressure, alternates between SLOPED segments (temperature rising within one phase, governed by q = mc delta-T) and FLAT PLATEAUS (temperature constant during a phase change, governed by q = n(delta-H-fusion or vaporization)). For water starting as ice at -20 C: a sloped segment warms ice to 0 C, a flat plateau at 0 C is melting, a sloped segment warms liquid water from 0 C to 100 C, a flat plateau at 100 C is boiling (this plateau is the LONGEST on the graph, reflecting vaporization's much larger latent heat), and a final sloped segment heats steam above 100 C. A student can read a heating curve's plateau widths directly to compare latent heats between substances, and the plateau's constant temperature is the empirical, historical basis for defining fixed points like 0 C and 100 C in the first place.

lessons.workedExample: How much energy is needed to convert 50.0 g of ice at -10 C into steam at 110 C? Four steps: (1) warm ice -10 to 0 C: q = (50.0 g)(2.09 J/g C)(10 C) = 1045 J. (2) melt ice at 0 C: q = (50.0 g)(334 J/g) = 16,700 J. (3) warm liquid 0 to 100 C: q = (50.0 g)(4.184 J/g C)(100 C) = 20,920 J. (4) boil at 100 C: q = (50.0 g)(2260 J/g) = 113,000 J. (5) warm steam 100 to 110 C: q = (50.0 g)(2.0 J/g C)(10 C) = 1000 J. Total: 1045 + 16,700 + 20,920 + 113,000 + 1000 = 152,665 J, about 153 kJ — and boiling alone (step 4) accounts for roughly 74% of the total energy, the clearest numerical demonstration of why vaporization dominates a heating curve's energy budget.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge probes heating-curve reasoning because it is a compact test of whether a student can correctly segment a multi-step energy calculation and knows WHERE temperature changes (sloped regions, q = mc delta-T) versus where it does not (plateaus, q = n delta-H). A strong answer identifies which step of a five-step calculation dominates the total energy and explains why (usually vaporization, due to breaking essentially all intermolecular attraction); a weak answer applies a single specific heat value across a phase change or forgets that temperature stays fixed during melting or boiling.

questions.prompt: On a heating curve, temperature stays constant during a phase change because the added heat is:

options.text: Being lost to the surroundings
Going entirely into breaking or forming intermolecular attractions rather than raising kinetic energy
Not actually being absorbed by the substance
Converting into electrical energy

explanations.a: The plateau reflects energy absorbed by the substance for the phase change itself, not heat loss to surroundings.
explanations.b: Correct — during a phase change, added energy restructures intermolecular attractions rather than increasing average molecular kinetic energy, so temperature (a measure of that kinetic energy) does not rise.
explanations.c: The substance is absorbing the heat; it is simply not converting it into a temperature increase during the transition.
explanations.d: There is no conversion into electrical energy in a simple heating-curve scenario.

questions.prompt: Water's latent heat of vaporization (about 40.7 kJ/mol) is roughly 6-7 times larger than its latent heat of fusion (6.01 kJ/mol) because:

options.text: Melting requires breaking essentially all intermolecular attraction, while boiling requires almost none
Boiling must fully separate molecules against nearly all intermolecular attraction, while melting only disrupts the rigid lattice while molecules stay close
Water has no hydrogen bonding in the liquid phase
The two values should actually be equal and the difference is measurement error

explanations.a: This has the comparison backward — it is boiling, not melting, that requires overcoming nearly all intermolecular attraction.
explanations.b: Correct — vaporization must separate molecules essentially completely, overcoming nearly all hydrogen bonding, while fusion only needs to disrupt the ordered solid lattice while attraction between neighboring molecules largely persists.
explanations.c: Liquid water retains extensive, dynamic hydrogen bonding; that is precisely why vaporizing it takes so much energy.
explanations.d: This is a real, well-established physical difference, not a measurement artifact.

questions.prompt: Order the five stages of heating ice at -10 C into steam at 110 C.

items.text: Warm solid ice from -10 C to 0 C
Melt ice at a constant 0 C
Warm liquid water from 0 C to 100 C
Boil liquid water at a constant 100 C
Warm steam from 100 C to 110 C

questions.explanation: A heating curve alternates sloped (single-phase warming) and flat (phase-change) segments in strict temperature order: warm the solid, melt it, warm the liquid, boil it, then warm the resulting gas.

questions.prompt: Match each heating-curve feature to the equation that governs it.

left.text: A sloped segment (single phase, temperature rising)
A flat plateau (phase change, temperature constant)

right.text: q = mc(delta-T)
q = n(delta-H-fusion or vaporization)

questions.explanation: Sloped regions involve temperature change within one phase and use specific heat capacity; flat plateaus involve a phase transition at constant temperature and use latent (molar) heat.

lessons.label: Free Energy in Practice: Delta-G, Q, and Coupling

sections.heading: Delta-G vs delta-G-standard, and the reaction quotient Q
sections.body: Delta-G-standard describes spontaneity only under STANDARD conditions (1 M concentrations for solutes, 1 bar for gases, 298 K). Real reactions almost never sit exactly at those conditions, so the actual, instantaneous delta-G is given by delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln(Q), where Q is the reaction quotient — calculated exactly like the equilibrium constant K, but using whatever concentrations or pressures actually exist at that moment, not necessarily equilibrium values. This equation is the bridge between thermodynamics and kinetics-adjacent reality: a reaction with a positive delta-G-standard (nonspontaneous under standard conditions) can still proceed spontaneously (delta-G negative) if Q is kept small enough — for instance, by continuously removing product so the reaction never approaches equilibrium, a strategy cells use constantly and industrial processes exploit by venting product gas.

sections.heading: Non-standard conditions in practice
sections.body: As a reaction proceeds toward equilibrium, Q changes continuously (moving from its starting value toward K), so delta-G shrinks in magnitude and reaches exactly zero at equilibrium (where Q equals K, making RT ln(Q/K) equal to zero) — this is why delta-G, unlike delta-G-standard, is not a fixed number for a given reaction but depends on exactly how far the system currently sits from equilibrium. A reaction can have a very unfavorable delta-G-standard yet still run forward under real cellular or industrial conditions simply because reactant concentrations are kept high and product concentrations low, keeping Q far below K and RT ln(Q) sufficiently negative to overcome a positive delta-G-standard. This is precisely how living cells drive many otherwise nonspontaneous biochemical steps: not by violating thermodynamics, but by controlling concentrations.

sections.heading: Coupled reactions — the ATP example
sections.body: Cells rarely rely on a single reaction's delta-G-standard being favorable; instead they COUPLE an unfavorable reaction to a strongly favorable one so the SUM of the two delta-G values is negative, even though each step individually might not be. The classic example is ATP hydrolysis, ATP + H2O to ADP + phosphate, with delta-G-standard around -30.5 kJ/mol (though the actual cellular delta-G, given real intracellular concentrations of ATP, ADP, phosphate, and Mg2+ that stabilizes ATP, is typically more negative, often cited near -50 kJ/mol). Cells couple this hydrolysis, via shared enzyme mechanisms and shared reaction intermediates, to biosynthetic steps that would otherwise be thermodynamically unfavorable — for example, the first step of glycolysis, phosphorylating glucose, has an unfavorable delta-G-standard on its own but becomes strongly favorable when coupled to ATP hydrolysis within the same enzyme active site.

lessons.workedExample: A reaction has delta-G-standard = +20.0 kJ/mol at 298 K. Its reaction quotient Q under current cellular conditions is 1.0 x 10^-6 (reactant-rich, product-poor). Compute the actual delta-G: delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln(Q) = 20,000 J/mol + (8.314 J/mol K)(298 K) ln(1.0 x 10^-6). Ln(1.0 x 10^-6) is about -13.8, so RT ln(Q) = (2477.6)(-13.8) = about -34,190 J/mol. Delta-G = 20,000 - 34,190 = -14,190 J/mol, or about -14.2 kJ/mol — negative, so the reaction proceeds spontaneously under these non-standard, product-depleted conditions despite its unfavorable standard free energy, which is exactly the mechanism cells rely on to run otherwise 'uphill' biosynthetic steps.
lessons.judgeFraming: A fair judge asks students to distinguish delta-G-standard from actual delta-G because this exact distinction is where 'is this reaction spontaneous' claims most often go wrong in a project write-up — students frequently cite a standard-condition delta-G-standard value from a table and treat it as if it describes their actual experimental or biological system. A strong answer explicitly invokes delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln(Q) and names how concentrations were kept away from equilibrium; a weak answer conflates delta-G-standard with delta-G or claims a reaction with positive delta-G-standard simply 'cannot happen,' ignoring the reaction-quotient term entirely.

questions.prompt: A reaction has an unfavorable (positive) delta-G-standard but can still proceed spontaneously under real conditions if:

options.text: Q is kept small enough that RT ln(Q) is sufficiently negative to make the overall delta-G negative
The temperature is lowered to absolute zero
The reaction is run at exactly standard conditions
Delta-G-standard is recalculated to be negative

explanations.a: Correct — delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln(Q); keeping reactants high and products low (small Q) makes the ln(Q) term strongly negative, which can outweigh a positive delta-G-standard.
explanations.b: Lowering temperature toward absolute zero does not by itself fix an unfavorable delta-G-standard, and is not a realistic strategy for cellular or industrial reactions.
explanations.c: At exactly standard conditions Q equals 1 and ln(Q) equals zero, so delta-G equals delta-G-standard, which remains unfavorable.
explanations.d: Delta-G-standard is a fixed thermodynamic quantity at a given temperature; it is not 'recalculated' to make a reaction proceed.

questions.prompt: At chemical equilibrium, delta-G equals zero because:

options.text: Delta-G-standard is always zero at equilibrium
Q equals K at equilibrium, making RT ln(Q/K) equal to zero
No reaction is occurring at all
Temperature must be exactly 298 K at equilibrium

explanations.a: Delta-G-standard is a fixed value at a given temperature and does not change as a reaction approaches equilibrium.
explanations.b: Correct — delta-G = delta-G-standard + RT ln(Q) = -RT ln(K) + RT ln(Q) = RT ln(Q/K), which is zero exactly when Q equals K, i.e. at equilibrium.
explanations.c: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; the reaction is dynamic, not stopped.
explanations.d: Equilibrium can occur at any temperature; 298 K is not a requirement.

questions.prompt: Order the logic a cell uses to drive an otherwise unfavorable biosynthetic step using ATP hydrolysis.

items.text: Identify a biosynthetic step with an unfavorable delta-G-standard on its own
Couple that step to ATP hydrolysis (delta-G-standard around -30.5 kJ/mol) via a shared enzyme mechanism
Sum the two delta-G values so the combined process is spontaneous overall

questions.explanation: Coupling requires first identifying the unfavorable step, then linking it mechanistically to a strongly favorable reaction like ATP hydrolysis, so that summing the two individual delta-G values yields an overall negative delta-G.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to what it describes.

right.text: Free energy change under standard 1 M / 1 bar / 298 K conditions; a fixed reference value
Actual free energy change under whatever concentrations currently exist, via delta-G-standard plus RT ln(Q)

questions.explanation: Delta-G-standard is a single reference value defined at standard conditions, while delta-G is the real, moment-to-moment free energy change that depends on the current reaction quotient Q.

lessons.label: Reaction Rate and Rate Laws

sections.heading: What reaction rate actually measures
sections.body: Reaction rate is the change in a species' concentration per unit time: rate = -Δ[reactant]/Δt = +Δ[product]/Δt, with each term divided by its stoichiometric coefficient so every expression for the same reaction agrees. The average rate over an interval is a secant-line slope on a concentration-versus-time graph; the instantaneous rate at one moment is the slope of the tangent line there, and it is this instantaneous value that rate laws describe. Units are mol/(L·s), written M/s, and rate is reported as a positive quantity by convention even though reactant concentrations are falling. For N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g), the single rate is expressed three equivalent ways: rate = -Δ[N2]/Δt = -(1/3)Δ[H2]/Δt = (1/2)Δ[NH3]/Δt, all describing the same physical process at the same moment.

sections.heading: The rate law and reaction order
sections.body: A differential rate law has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are the reaction orders with respect to A and B. The critical, often-missed point is that m and n must be measured experimentally — they are NOT read off the balanced equation's coefficients, a fact that surprised early kineticists since intuition suggests stoichiometry should dictate rate directly. The overall order is m + n, and while orders are usually small whole numbers, mechanisms involving reactive intermediates or chain processes can produce fractional orders. The rate constant k is temperature-dependent and its units shift with overall order (M/s for zero order, s⁻¹ for first order, M⁻¹s⁻¹ for second order) so that rate itself always comes out in M/s regardless of the rate law's form.

sections.heading: Extracting order from initial-rate data
sections.body: The method of initial rates isolates each order experimentally: run several trials, changing one reactant's starting concentration at a time while holding the others fixed, and measure the INITIAL rate of each trial (before meaningful reactant depletion, so the concentrations used are still accurate). Comparing the ratio of rates between two trials to the ratio of that one concentration reveals the order: unchanged rate means order 0, a doubled rate for a doubled concentration means order 1, a quadrupled rate for a doubled concentration means order 2, and so on for other ratios. Once every order is known, substituting any single trial's rate and concentrations back into the rate law solves for k.

lessons.workedExample: Consider 2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g). Trial 1: [NO]=0.10 M, [O2]=0.10 M, initial rate=0.0080 M/s. Trial 2: [NO]=0.20 M, [O2]=0.10 M (only [NO] doubled), rate=0.032 M/s — a four-fold jump, so the reaction is second order in NO. Trial 3: [NO]=0.10 M, [O2]=0.20 M (only [O2] doubled), rate=0.016 M/s — exactly double, so first order in O2. The rate law is rate=k[NO]^2[O2], overall third order; using Trial 1, k=0.0080/(0.10^2×0.10)=8.0 M⁻²s⁻¹. Note the measured exponents happen to equal the balanced equation's coefficients here — that is a coincidence of this particular reaction, never a rule to assume in advance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who understands kinetics will ask a team to justify why they assumed a particular rate law, especially if they simply copied stoichiometric coefficients into exponents. A strong answer cites the actual initial-rate data used, walks through how doubling one reagent's concentration changed the measured rate, and correctly states the units of k for the given overall order. A weak answer says "the rate law comes from the balanced equation" — a common misconception — or cannot explain why NO2 is squared in the rate expression above. Judges probe this because it is the single most-confused idea in kinetics, separating rote pattern matching from real experimental understanding.

questions.prompt: For the reaction 2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g), doubling [NO] while holding [O2] constant increases the initial rate four-fold. What is the order of the reaction with respect to NO?

options.text: Zero order
First order
Second order
Third order

explanations.a: Zero order would mean the rate does not change at all when [NO] doubles, but the rate quadrupled.
explanations.b: First order would mean the rate exactly doubles when [NO] doubles, but it quadrupled instead.
explanations.c: A four-fold rate increase from a two-fold concentration increase means rate is proportional to [NO]^2, i.e., second order in NO (2^2 = 4).
explanations.d: Third order would require an eight-fold rate increase (2^3 = 8) when [NO] doubles, not four-fold.

questions.prompt: Which statement about determining a rate law is correct?

options.text: The exponents in the rate law always equal the coefficients in the balanced equation.
The exponents in the rate law must be determined experimentally and can differ from the stoichiometric coefficients.
The rate constant k has the same units regardless of the overall reaction order.
A reaction's overall order is always a whole number.

explanations.a: This is a common misconception — coefficients only sometimes match observed orders, and only experiment can confirm it.
explanations.b: Correct: reaction order is an experimental quantity, found from how rate responds to concentration changes, and can differ from stoichiometry.
explanations.c: Incorrect — k's units depend on overall order (e.g., s⁻¹ for first order, M⁻¹s⁻¹ for second order) so that rate always comes out in M/s.
explanations.d: Incorrect — some mechanisms (especially chain reactions or those with reactive intermediates) give fractional orders.

questions.prompt: Put the method-of-initial-rates procedure in the correct order for determining a rate law from experimental data.

items.text: Run multiple trials, changing one reactant's concentration at a time while holding the others fixed
Measure the initial rate of each trial before significant reactant is consumed
Compare the ratio of rates to the ratio of concentrations to find each order
Use one trial's rate, concentrations, and orders to solve for the rate constant k

questions.explanation: You must first design trials that isolate one variable, then measure the resulting initial rates, then use those ratios to extract each order, and only at the end solve for k using the now-known rate law.

questions.prompt: Match each overall reaction order to the units of its rate constant k (concentration in mol/L, time in seconds).

right.text: M/s (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹)
s⁻¹
M⁻¹ s⁻¹ (L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹)

questions.explanation: Since rate is always in M/s, k's units must cancel whatever concentration powers appear in the rate law: zero order has no concentration term so k is already in M/s; first order divides M/s by M leaving s⁻¹; second order divides M/s by M^2 leaving M⁻¹ s⁻¹.

lessons.label: Integrated Rate Laws and Half-Life

sections.heading: First-order integrated law and constant half-life
sections.body: Integrating the differential first-order rate law, rate=-d[A]/dt=k[A], gives ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt (equivalently [A]t=[A]0e^(-kt)). Its defining feature is a half-life, t1/2=ln2/k≈0.693/k, that is completely independent of starting concentration — a first-order process always takes the same amount of time to fall to half of whatever concentration it currently has. This constant half-life is why first-order kinetics describes radioactive decay, and why the thermal decomposition of gaseous N2O5 (2N2O5(g) -> 4NO2(g) + O2(g)), one of the most historically studied gas-phase reactions in kinetics, is a textbook first-order example: a plot of ln[N2O5] against time comes out as a straight line, confirming the order experimentally rather than assuming it from the equation.

sections.heading: Zero- and second-order integrated laws
sections.body: The zero-order integrated law, [A]t=[A]0-kt, is linear in [A] itself; because concentration falls at a constant rate, its half-life, t1/2=[A]0/(2k), shrinks every time it is recalculated from a lower starting concentration. Zero-order kinetics appears when rate is limited by something other than reactant concentration, such as a fixed number of catalytic surface sites or an enzyme running at saturating substrate. The second-order integrated law, 1/[A]t=1/[A]0+kt, is linear in the reciprocal concentration, and its half-life, t1/2=1/(k[A]0), grows longer as the reaction proceeds — each successive halving takes more time at ever lower concentration, the opposite behavior from first order.

sections.heading: Using linearized plots to identify order
sections.body: Because each order's integrated law is linear in a different transformed variable, the same concentration-versus-time data is plotted three ways: [A] vs t, ln[A] vs t, and 1/[A] vs t. Whichever plot comes out straight (by inspection or a linear-regression R² close to 1) reveals the true order — a far more reliable diagnostic than trying to guess order from a curved raw concentration-versus-time trace alone, since first- and second-order decay curves can look deceptively similar over a short observation window.

lessons.workedExample: A first-order decomposition has k=0.0450 min⁻¹. Its half-life is t1/2=0.693/0.0450=15.4 min, meaning the concentration falls by half every 15.4 minutes no matter how much is present. Starting from [A]0=0.800 M, the concentration after 30.0 minutes (just under two half-lives) is found from ln[A]=ln(0.800)-(0.0450)(30.0)=-0.223-1.35=-1.573, so [A]=e^(-1.573)=0.207 M — close to the 0.200 M expected from exactly two half-lives (0.800 -> 0.400 -> 0.200 M), the small difference arising because 30.0 min is slightly less than 2×15.4=30.8 min.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing integrated rate laws wants to know whether a team can distinguish "the reaction slowed down" from "the reaction is first order," since zero- and second-order reactions also slow as reactant depletes. The diagnostic question is always about half-life: does it stay constant (first order), shrink (zero order), or grow (second order)? A strong team can state which linearized plot they used to confirm order and why a curved raw concentration-versus-time graph alone would not have been convincing. A weak team assumes order from the balanced equation instead of from their own linearized data.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes first-order half-life from zero- and second-order half-life behavior?

options.text: First-order half-life is constant regardless of starting concentration; zero-order half-life shrinks over the reaction; second-order half-life grows over the reaction.
All three orders have a half-life that is constant regardless of concentration.
First-order half-life grows over time while zero- and second-order half-lives stay constant.
Half-life cannot be defined for zero- or second-order reactions.

explanations.a: Correct — this is the key diagnostic: t1/2=0.693/k (first order, constant) vs [A]0/(2k) (zero order, shrinks as the starting concentration used for the next half-life is lower) vs 1/(k[A]0) (second order, grows).
explanations.b: Only first-order half-life is independent of concentration; the other two both depend on concentration, just in opposite directions.
explanations.c: This has it backwards — first order is the one with constant half-life.
explanations.d: Half-life is defined for all three orders; only its dependence on concentration differs.

questions.prompt: A plot of ln[A] versus time is linear for a certain reaction, but a plot of [A] versus time is curved. What is the reaction order?

options.text: Zero order
First order
Second order
Cannot be determined from this information

explanations.a: Zero order would make [A] vs t itself linear, not ln[A] vs t.
explanations.b: Correct — the first-order integrated law ln[A]=ln[A]0-kt is exactly the equation of a line when ln[A] is plotted against t.
explanations.c: Second order gives a linear plot of 1/[A] vs t, not ln[A] vs t.
explanations.d: The linearity of ln[A] vs t is precisely the diagnostic test for first order — it can be determined.

questions.prompt: Order the steps used to determine a reaction's order from raw concentration-versus-time data using linearized plots.

items.text: Collect [A] at several time points during the reaction
Plot [A] vs t, ln[A] vs t, and 1/[A] vs t
Identify which of the three plots is linear
Read the order (0, 1, or 2) and slope (±k) off the linear plot

questions.explanation: Data collection must come first; then all three transformed plots are made side by side; only after seeing which one straightens out can the order be identified; the slope of that one linear plot then gives k.

questions.prompt: Match each reaction order to its correct integrated rate law.

right.text: [A]t = [A]0 - kt
ln[A]t = ln[A]0 - kt

questions.explanation: Each order's integrated law comes from integrating its differential rate law: zero order (rate=k) gives a linear equation in [A] itself; first order (rate=k[A]) gives a linear equation in ln[A]; second order (rate=k[A]^2) gives a linear equation in 1/[A].

lessons.label: Collision Theory and Activation Energy

sections.heading: The collision model of reaction rate
sections.body: Collision theory holds that a reaction can only occur when reactant particles physically collide, so rate depends on collision frequency, which is itself set by concentration and temperature. But not every collision reacts: molecular speeds (and thus kinetic energies) at any temperature follow a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, a spread of energies rather than one fixed value, and only the fraction of collisions with combined kinetic energy at or above a threshold called the activation energy, Ea, can actually break and reform bonds. Raising the temperature shifts the whole distribution toward higher energies and, critically, disproportionately increases the fraction sitting above Ea — which is why modest temperature increases can produce large rate increases even though collision frequency itself grows only mildly with temperature.

sections.heading: Orientation: why most energetic collisions still fail
sections.body: Having enough energy is necessary but not sufficient. Reacting particles must also collide in a geometry that lines up the correct atoms or orbitals, described by the steric (orientation) factor, p, in the full collision-theory rate expression. For simple atoms this factor can be close to 1, but for larger, more complex molecules it is often far smaller, sometimes 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶, because only a narrow range of approach angles brings the reactive atoms together correctly. This is part of why collision theory alone, without an orientation correction, badly overpredicts rates for reactions between complex molecules, and why more detailed treatments, especially transition-state theory, were developed to handle geometry more rigorously.

sections.heading: Activation energy as an energy barrier
sections.body: Plotting potential energy against reaction progress shows that reactants must climb over a maximum, the transition state or activated complex, a fleeting, high-energy arrangement where old bonds are partly broken and new ones partly formed, before descending to products. The barrier's height above the reactants is the forward Ea, and its height above the products is the reverse Ea; the difference between them is the reaction's overall energy change (exothermic if products sit lower, endothermic if higher). The concept, and the term "activation energy," was introduced by Svante Arrhenius in 1889, building on earlier empirical work by Jacobus van't Hoff on how rate constants vary with temperature.

lessons.workedExample: The classic H2(g) + I2(g) -> 2HI(g) reaction has an experimentally measured activation energy of roughly 165 kJ/mol. At room temperature, 298 K, RT=(8.314 J/mol·K)(298 K)≈2.48 kJ/mol, so Ea/RT≈165/2.48≈66.6 — meaning the Boltzmann factor e^(-Ea/RT), which estimates the fraction of collisions with enough energy, is roughly e^(-66.6), an almost vanishingly small fraction. This is why, despite enormous numbers of collisions per second, the uncatalyzed reaction is slow at room temperature; it is also why this specific reaction is historically important — later work (J. H. Sullivan, 1967) showed its true mechanism is more complex than a single bimolecular collision, involving iodine atoms as intermediates.
lessons.judgeFraming: This concept is a favorite judge probe because it separates memorized vocabulary from real mechanistic reasoning. A judge will ask why raising temperature by only 10°C can double a rate, and a strong answer explains it through the shifting Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and the exponential sensitivity of the fraction above Ea, not just "molecules move faster." A judge may also ask why two molecules with plenty of energy still fail to react, testing whether the team understands orientation as a separate requirement from energy. Reciting "activation energy is the energy needed to react" without explaining the barrier or the distribution is a weak answer.

questions.prompt: According to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, why does a modest increase in temperature often cause a large increase in reaction rate?

options.text: Because all molecules move exactly the same amount faster
Because the fraction of collisions with energy at or above the activation energy increases disproportionately as the whole energy distribution shifts
Because activation energy itself decreases as temperature rises
Because collision frequency increases by the same large factor as the rate

explanations.a: The distribution is a spread, not a single speed, and it broadens and shifts unevenly, not uniformly.
explanations.b: Correct — the high-energy tail of the distribution above Ea grows disproportionately fast as temperature rises, which is the real source of the large rate increase.
explanations.c: Ea is a property of the reaction pathway and does not change with temperature.
explanations.d: Collision frequency itself increases only mildly (roughly with the square root of T); the large rate increase comes from the energy distribution, not collision frequency.

questions.prompt: Two molecules collide with kinetic energy well above the activation energy but the reaction does not occur. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Activation energy does not apply to this collision
The molecules were not correctly oriented for the reactive atoms to meet
The reaction is exothermic
The rate constant is zero

explanations.a: Activation energy always applies; having enough energy is necessary but not sufficient.
explanations.b: Correct — collision theory's orientation (steric) factor accounts for exactly this: energy alone is not enough without proper geometric alignment.
explanations.c: Exothermic vs endothermic describes overall energy change, not why a single collision failed.
explanations.d: A zero rate constant would mean the reaction never occurs at all, which is not implied by one failed collision.

questions.prompt: Order the events of a single successful reactive collision, from approach to separated products.

items.text: Two reactant particles approach with combined kinetic energy at or above Ea
The particles collide with the correct orientation to bring reactive atoms together
Old bonds partially break and new bonds partially form at the transition state (activated complex)
Products form and separate, releasing or absorbing energy relative to the reactants

questions.explanation: Sufficient energy and correct orientation are both prerequisites for the collision to reach the transition state at all; only after the activated complex forms can bonds finish rearranging into separated products.

questions.prompt: Match each collision-theory term to its correct description.

right.text: The minimum combined kinetic energy reacting particles need for a collision to result in reaction
The fleeting, highest-energy arrangement partway between reactants and products, where bonds are partly broken and partly formed
A correction factor accounting for the fact that particles must collide in a specific geometric alignment to react

questions.explanation: Ea sets the energy threshold, the transition state is the specific high-energy configuration at the top of that energy barrier, and the steric factor separately captures the geometric requirement that energy alone does not guarantee.

lessons.label: The Arrhenius Equation and Temperature

sections.heading: The Arrhenius equation
sections.body: In 1889, Svante Arrhenius proposed k=Ae^(-Ea/RT), tying collision theory directly to a measurable rate constant. R is the gas constant (8.314 J/(mol·K)), T is absolute temperature, Ea is activation energy, and A is the pre-exponential (or frequency) factor — a term bundling together how often molecules collide and how favorably they are oriented, effectively standing in for collision frequency and the steric factor combined. The exponential term e^(-Ea/RT) is exactly the Boltzmann-factor estimate of the fraction of collisions energetic enough to react, so the whole equation reads as: rate constant = (how often and how well-aligned particles collide) × (what fraction of those collisions have enough energy).

sections.heading: Why rate is so sensitive to temperature
sections.body: Because Ea sits inside an exponential, k (and therefore rate) is far more sensitive to temperature than to a concentration change of similar relative size. A widely used classroom rule of thumb, that rate roughly doubles for every 10°C rise near room temperature, holds only approximately, and only for reactions with Ea in the range typical of many organic and inorganic reactions (roughly 50-100 kJ/mol); reactions with very low or very high Ea deviate substantially from that "doubling" heuristic, since the real relationship is set by the size of Ea/RT, not a universal constant.

sections.heading: The Arrhenius plot and finding Ea from data
sections.body: Taking the natural log of both sides gives ln k = -(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A, a linear equation in 1/T with slope -Ea/R and y-intercept ln A. Measuring k at several temperatures and plotting ln k against 1/T, an "Arrhenius plot," lets a straight-line fit yield both Ea and A without ever measuring collision frequency directly. When only two (k, T) data points are available, the same relationship reduces to the two-point form ln(k2/k1) = -(Ea/R)(1/T2 - 1/T1), solved directly for Ea.

lessons.workedExample: A reaction has k1=3.0×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at T1=300 K and k2=8.3×10⁻³ s⁻¹ at T2=340 K. Using the two-point Arrhenius equation: ln(k2/k1)=ln(8.3×10⁻³/3.0×10⁻⁴)=ln(27.7)=3.32. Then (1/T1-1/T2)=(1/300-1/340)=0.003333-0.002941=3.92×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Solving Ea=R·ln(k2/k1)/(1/T1-1/T2)=(8.314 J/mol·K)(3.32)/(3.92×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹)≈70,400 J/mol≈70.4 kJ/mol. This Ea, once known, could then be used with either original (k,T) pair to back out the pre-exponential factor A from the one-point form of the equation.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge listening to a kinetics-heavy project will often ask a team to explain, in words, why their measured rate roughly doubled when they ran their reaction 10 degrees warmer, and whether that doubling is a law or a rule of thumb. A strong answer connects the observation back to Ea sitting inside an exponential and can sketch how an Arrhenius plot of ln k versus 1/T would be used to extract Ea from their own data. A weak answer treats "rate doubles every 10 degrees" as an exact universal law rather than an approximation that depends on the reaction's specific Ea.

questions.prompt: In the Arrhenius equation k=Ae^(-Ea/RT), what does the pre-exponential factor A represent?

options.text: The fraction of collisions with sufficient energy to react
A term reflecting collision frequency and molecular orientation, roughly independent of the energy barrier itself
The activation energy divided by the gas constant
The equilibrium constant of the reaction

explanations.a: That fraction is captured by the exponential term e^(-Ea/RT), not by A.
explanations.b: Correct — A bundles collision frequency and orientation (steric) effects together, separate from the energy-barrier term.
explanations.c: Ea/R has units of temperature and appears only inside the exponent, not as A.
explanations.d: A is unrelated to the equilibrium constant; it is a kinetic, not thermodynamic, quantity.

questions.prompt: Why is reaction rate typically far more sensitive to a change in temperature than to a similarly sized relative change in reactant concentration?

options.text: Because temperature changes A but concentration does not
Because temperature appears inside an exponential term with Ea, while concentration enters the rate law only as a power
Because concentration has no effect on collision frequency
Because Ea decreases as temperature increases

explanations.a: A is treated as roughly constant over modest temperature ranges in the simple Arrhenius picture; that is not the main sensitivity mechanism.
explanations.b: Correct — k depends on T exponentially, through e^(-Ea/RT), so small T changes shift k a lot, whereas concentration only enters as [A]^m, a much gentler power-law dependence.
explanations.c: Concentration does affect collision frequency; that is exactly why it appears in the rate law, but its effect is polynomial, not exponential.
explanations.d: Ea is a property of the reaction pathway and does not change with temperature.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for finding Ea from two experimentally measured (k, T) pairs using the two-point Arrhenius equation.

items.text: Measure the rate constant k at two different temperatures T1 and T2
Compute ln(k2/k1)
Compute (1/T1 - 1/T2)
Solve Ea = R·ln(k2/k1) / (1/T1 - 1/T2)

questions.explanation: The two-point equation needs both raw (k,T) measurements first; then the log-ratio of the rate constants and the difference of the reciprocal temperatures are each computed separately before being combined to isolate Ea.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol in the Arrhenius equation k = A·e^(-Ea/RT) to what it represents.

right.text: Pre-exponential (frequency) factor combining collision frequency and orientation
Activation energy, the energy barrier reactants must clear
The gas constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K)
Absolute temperature in kelvin

questions.explanation: Each symbol plays a distinct role: A carries the collision/orientation information, Ea sets the energy threshold, R is the universal constant converting energy and temperature units consistently, and T is the absolute temperature that drives the exponential term.

lessons.label: Reaction Mechanisms and the Rate-Determining Step

sections.heading: Elementary steps and molecularity
sections.body: A reaction mechanism proposes a sequence of elementary steps, individual molecular-level events, that sum to the overall balanced equation. Unlike an overall reaction, an elementary step's rate law CAN be written directly from its stoichiometry, because it describes one specific molecular collision or rearrangement: a unimolecular step (one molecule reacting alone, as in a rearrangement or decomposition) has rate=k[A]; a bimolecular step (two particles colliding) has rate=k[A][B] or k[A]^2; a termolecular step (three particles colliding simultaneously) is possible in principle but rare in practice, since the odds of three particles meeting at exactly the right place, time, and orientation are far lower than for two.

sections.heading: Intermediates and the rate-determining step
sections.body: A species produced in one step and fully consumed in a later step, never appearing in the overall balanced equation or among the initial reactants, is a reaction intermediate. When a mechanism has one step markedly slower than the others, that slow step is the rate-determining step (RDS), and it alone sets the overall rate law, since the fast steps around it do not limit how quickly the sequence proceeds. If the RDS itself involves an intermediate rather than only original reactants, that intermediate's concentration must be re-expressed in terms of original reactants, often via a pre-equilibrium approximation applied to a preceding fast, reversible step, before the derived rate law can be compared to the experimentally measured one.

sections.heading: A worked mechanism: NO2 + CO
sections.body: The reaction NO2(g) + CO(g) -> NO(g) + CO2(g) has an experimentally measured low-temperature rate law of rate=k[NO2]^2, with no dependence on [CO] at all, inconsistent with a single-step bimolecular collision between NO2 and CO. A two-step mechanism proposed by Ogg in 1947 resolves this: Step 1 (slow), NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO; Step 2 (fast), NO3 + CO -> NO2 + CO2. NO3 is the intermediate, produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2; the two steps sum correctly to the overall reaction, and since the slow step alone involves only NO2 (twice), its rate law, k[NO2]^2, matches the experimental result exactly.

lessons.workedExample: Verify the NO2 + CO mechanism against experiment. Summing the elementary steps, (NO2+NO2->NO3+NO) + (NO3+CO->NO2+CO2), gives 2NO2+NO3+CO -> NO3+NO+NO2+CO2; canceling one NO2 and the NO3 that appears on both sides leaves NO2+CO -> NO+CO2, exactly the overall observed reaction. Because step 1 is the slow (rate-determining) step and involves two NO2 molecules colliding, its rate law is rate=k[NO2]^2, with no [CO] term at all, since CO only reacts in the fast second step, after the rate has already been set by the slow first step. This matches the experimentally measured rate law, confirming the mechanism at low-to-moderate temperature.
lessons.judgeFraming: Mechanism questions test whether a team understands that a proposed mechanism is a hypothesis to be checked against data, not a story invented to sound plausible. A judge will ask: does your mechanism sum to the correct overall equation? Does its rate-determining step predict the SAME rate law you actually measured, including which species are absent from it? A strong answer can point to a specific intermediate and explain why it drops out of the overall equation and, if relevant, out of the final rate law. A weak answer proposes a mechanism but never checks it against either the stoichiometry or the measured kinetics.

questions.prompt: In the two-step mechanism for NO2 + CO -> NO + CO2 (Step 1, slow: NO2+NO2->NO3+NO; Step 2, fast: NO3+CO->NO2+CO2), what role does NO3 play?

options.text: It is a catalyst
It is a reaction intermediate
It is the rate-determining species that appears in the final rate law
It is a spectator ion

explanations.a: A catalyst is present unchanged at the start and end and lowers Ea for both steps; NO3 is instead produced then fully consumed within the mechanism, never added to the system as a starting reagent.
explanations.b: Correct — NO3 is generated in step 1 and completely consumed in step 2, so it cancels out of the overall equation, the definition of an intermediate.
explanations.c: The measured rate law is k[NO2]^2 and contains no NO3 term at all, since NO3 does not appear until after the rate-determining step.
explanations.d: "Spectator ion" describes an ionic species unchanged by a reaction in solution, not a covalent intermediate generated and consumed across mechanism steps.

questions.prompt: Why does the experimentally measured rate law for NO2 + CO, rate=k[NO2]^2, contain no [CO] term even though CO is a reactant in the overall equation?

options.text: CO does not participate in the mechanism at all
CO only reacts in the fast second step, after the slow first step (involving only NO2) has already set the overall rate
CO's concentration is always exactly 1 M in this reaction
The rate law was measured incorrectly

explanations.a: CO does participate, in step 2; it is simply not part of the rate-determining step.
explanations.b: Correct — since the slow step is rate-limiting, whatever happens afterward, like CO reacting with NO3 in the fast step, does not show up in the overall rate law.
explanations.c: Rate laws reflect kinetic order, not a fixed numerical concentration; even if [CO]=1 M, order in CO would still show up mathematically if it affected rate.
explanations.d: An RDS-based rate law lacking a term for a species that only reacts after the RDS is expected behavior, not an error.

questions.prompt: Order the general steps used to test whether a proposed multi-step mechanism is consistent with an experimentally measured rate law.

items.text: Sum all elementary steps and cancel intermediates to confirm they add up to the overall balanced equation
Identify the slowest (rate-determining) step
Write the rate law directly from the stoichiometry of that rate-determining step
If the rate-determining step contains an intermediate, substitute it out using a preceding fast equilibrium, then compare the resulting rate law to the experimental one

questions.explanation: A mechanism must first be checked for correct overall stoichiometry; only then does identifying the slow step make sense; the rate law follows directly from that step's molecularity; and if an intermediate remains in that expression, it must be replaced with reactant terms before the final comparison to experiment.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism-related term to its correct meaning.

right.text: A single molecular-level event whose rate law can be written directly from its own stoichiometry
The number of particles that must collide or rearrange within one elementary step (uni-, bi-, or termolecular)
A species produced in one step and fully consumed in a later step, absent from the overall equation
The slowest step in a mechanism, which alone controls the overall rate law

questions.explanation: These four terms build on each other: a mechanism is made of elementary steps, each with a molecularity; species that cancel across steps are intermediates; and whichever step is slowest dictates the rate law for the whole sequence.

lessons.label: Catalysis

sections.heading: Homogeneous versus heterogeneous catalysts
sections.body: A homogeneous catalyst exists in the same phase as the reactants, typically dissolved in the same solution or mixed in the same gas phase, and participates directly in an elementary step before being regenerated. A striking real example is stratospheric ozone destruction by chlorine radicals: Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2, followed by ClO + O -> Cl + O2, regenerating the Cl atom to attack another O3 molecule. Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland proposed this catalytic cycle in 1974 (work that, with Paul Crutzen, earned the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), showing that CFC-derived chlorine atoms could each destroy many thousands of ozone molecules before being removed from the stratosphere. Heterogeneous catalysts, by contrast, are in a different phase from the reactants, almost always a solid surface acting on gas- or solution-phase reactants, as in the Haber process's iron catalyst or the platinum-group-metal beds used in catalytic converters.

sections.heading: Enzymes as biological catalysts
sections.body: Enzymes are protein (or, in some cases, RNA) catalysts that bind a specific substrate at an active site shaped to stabilize the transition state of the reaction being catalyzed, a picture refined from the original rigid "lock-and-key" model into Daniel Koshland's more accurate "induced fit," in which the active site subtly reshapes around the substrate as it binds. Enzymes can be extraordinarily effective: catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide (2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2), is among the fastest known enzymes, processing tens of millions of substrate molecules per second per enzyme molecule, accelerating that decomposition by many orders of magnitude relative to the uncatalyzed reaction.

sections.heading: How a catalyst actually lowers activation energy
sections.body: A catalyst works by providing an entirely different reaction pathway, a different sequence of elementary steps with different (lower) transition states, rather than by pumping energy into the existing pathway. On an energy diagram, the catalyzed path's peaks sit lower than the uncatalyzed path's single peak, so a larger fraction of collisions clears the now-smaller barrier. Crucially, a catalyst lowers Ea for the forward AND reverse reactions equally, meaning it speeds up the approach to equilibrium without shifting where that equilibrium lies: it changes the reaction's rate, not its ΔH or its equilibrium constant.

sections.heading: Catalytic converters: heterogeneous catalysis at work
sections.body: The three-way catalytic converter in a gasoline car's exhaust system uses a ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum-group metals to run two families of reactions at once: platinum and palladium oxidize carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons (2CO+O2->2CO2), while rhodium reduces nitrogen oxides back to harmless N2 and O2. The honeycomb's huge surface area maximizes contact between gas and metal, but the catalyst needs to reach a minimum "light-off" temperature, roughly 250-300°C, before it becomes effective, which is why a cold engine start produces disproportionately more tailpipe pollution than the same engine once warmed up.

lessons.workedExample: In a warmed-up catalytic converter, exhaust gas containing CO, unburned hydrocarbons, and NO passes over a Pt/Pd/Rh-coated ceramic honeycomb. On the oxidation sites, 2CO(g)+O2(g)->2CO2(g), and hydrocarbons are similarly oxidized to CO2 and H2O; on the separate reduction sites, 2NO(g)->N2(g)+O2(g). None of the metal is consumed; it is regenerated as each molecule desorbs, ready to bind and convert the next one, the defining feature of any catalyst. If the same engine is started cold, exhaust passes through before the honeycomb reaches its roughly 250-300°C light-off temperature, so a much larger fraction of CO, hydrocarbons, and NOx exits unconverted, the reason cold-start emissions testing is weighted so heavily in vehicle emissions regulations.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge testing catalysis understanding will ask the precise mechanistic question: does the catalyst provide more energy, or a lower-energy pathway? A strong answer explains the alternative-pathway/lower-transition-state picture and can state clearly that a catalyst does not change ΔH or the equilibrium constant, only the rate of reaching it. Judges also probe whether a team can name a real catalyst relevant to their project, an enzyme, a converter's metal, an industrial catalyst, rather than speaking only in the abstract. A weak answer says a catalyst "gives the reaction energy" or "makes the reaction go further," both of which confuse kinetics with thermodynamics.

questions.prompt: What is the fundamental mechanism by which a catalyst increases reaction rate?

options.text: It supplies additional energy directly to the reactant molecules
It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the concentration of the reactants
It shifts the reaction's equilibrium toward products

explanations.a: A catalyst does not add energy to the system; the reaction still proceeds using the same thermal energy available in the surroundings.
explanations.b: Correct — a catalyst opens a different mechanistic route whose transition state(s) sit at lower energy, so more collisions clear the barrier at a given temperature.
explanations.c: Catalysts are not consumed and do not change how much reactant is present; they act on the pathway, not the concentration.
explanations.d: A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally and does not move the equilibrium position at all.

questions.prompt: How does adding a catalyst affect a reaction's equilibrium constant, K, and overall enthalpy change, ΔH?

options.text: It increases K but leaves ΔH unchanged
It leaves both K and ΔH unchanged, since it speeds forward and reverse rates equally without altering the energetics of reactants or products
It decreases ΔH, making the reaction more exothermic
It increases both K and ΔH
